name: Northeast Rib (1951 Route)
beta: Two start variations exist: the original 1951 Route, which is faster but includes a 'scary' 5.7 pitch, and a 1957 variation that starts lower and adds roughly 500 ft of climbing on more logical terrain to avoid it. On the 1957 line, initial 4th-class terrain leads into dense vertical tree-root climbing, a slabby ~60-ft horizontal gully traverse (5.5) with minimal protection, and steep heather sections requiring careful, finger-pressing technique. On the right-hand (1957) rib, a roughly 700-ft crux section of higher-quality 5.6 rock climbing leads toward a bivy site beside the glacier, below the snow arete and glacier that lead to the summit.
overview: A parallel, marginally easier line to the Northeast Buttress up the same 5,000-ft face, first climbed in 1951 with a 1957 variation start; mostly unroped 3rd/4th-class climbing through a 'dangerous jungle gym' of vertical brush, with a sustained roughly 700-ft crux rock band on the 1957 variation's right-hand rib.

current.approach: From the Cascade Pass trailhead, descend to and cross the Cascade River, cross the terminal moraine, then downclimb into an avalanche moat to gain the rock and reach the base of the rib — a quick approach directly from the car.
approach_variant_names: Down into the avalanche moat before the couloir narrows, then the left-hand rib
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb the East Ridge's loose 3rd/4th-class ledges to the Cascade-Johannesburg col, rappelling a series of slings where needed. From the col, follow Doug's Direct: sidehill through wildflower meadows onto 45-60° heather slopes, cross to the north ridge of Mixup Peak, then descend the Cache Glacier back to the Cascade Pass trail — a three-part descent of roughly 1,600 ft that most parties find takes 4-6 hours total; the steep heather section is frequently cited as the most dangerous part of the entire trip.
current.detailed_rack: A small rock rack (frequently unusable in the loose/vegetated terrain) and a light rope.
current.pro_needs: Protection is frequently unusable through the vegetated and loose sections — much of the route should be treated as run-out; save gear for the ~700-ft crux rock band where placements are better.

name: Junior's Farm
beta: Start on the Bad-Tempered Prom Queen pitch (5.8+/FA: John Goodrum) located on a low-angle bulge just left of vine maple, serving as the approach to the upper pitches. Longer pitches include approximately 10-11 clips. Pitches 1 and 6 are notably stiff 5.8s. Fixed lines assist with the traverse between pitches 4-5. Plan for 6+ hours total for ascent and descent. The route is hot in summer—climb early in the day. Communication between climber and belayer may be difficult on upper pitches in wind.
overview: Junior's Farm is an eight-pitch alpine climbing route on the Mossness Wall featuring a mix of sport and traditional climbing with pitches ranging from 5.6 to 5.8. The route includes traverse and scramble sections between pitches and concludes with scrambling above the eighth pitch to reach the summit plateau.

current.approach: From the parking pullout on spur 270, an unmarked climbers' path ascends directly up the boulder field on the hillside toward Tyler Peak Crags; there is no formal trailhead sign. The Full Montey sits on the upper bench of the Tyler Peak crag system, reached by climbing up past the base of the adjacent Mossness wall/sector to gain the upper bench. Because the approach trail is unofficial and unsigned, most parties rely on a written area description or GPS beta rather than a marked trail; expect a steep, brushy bushwhack-and-boulder-hop of a few hundred vertical feet from the road.
current.descent: After completing pitch 8 and scrambling to the upper summit plateau area, descend via rappelling from the grassy ledge area at the base of the upper pitches. This area has established rappel anchors. Due to the terrain and pitch length, multiple rappels are required—7 rappels on a 60 m rope, or 6 on a 70 m. A single 60m rope is enough provided you use every anchor station; do not skip or link stations. Do not rely solely on fixed lines if present, as they may be unreliable. Verify all anchor points independently.
current.detailed_rack: A standard rock climbing rack suitable for 5.8-5.9 sport and trad climbing. Primary protection should be quickdraws (12-15 recommended for longer pitches). For trad sections, carry a full set of climbing nuts (BD.3 through BD.3 carabiners or equivalent), slings (60cm and 120cm), and 1-2 passive cams if available. Many pitches have fixed bolts, but fixed gear should not be the sole reliance. Ensure rappel anchors are verified before weighting—carry redundant sling and carabiner systems.
current.pro_needs: Protection on this route is mixed sport and trad. Most pitches have bolted anchors, but bolts should be supplemented with traditional gear on traverse and scramble sections. The upper pitches (6-8) benefit from redundant protection. Ensure adequate slings and carabiners for building solid anchor systems on grassy ledge areas where rock quality may be variable.
current.rope_note: Published descriptions list this as an 8-pitch Sport/Alpine route at Tyler Peak Crags (The Full Montey); a 70m rope suits typical Olympic Peninsula sport-alpine pitch lengths, though exact pitch lengths weren't published.

name: Just Enough
beta: Two parallel bolts partway up allow going right or left around mini-roofs — left is the recommended line. About 20 ft of sustained climbing; most of the rest is easier.
overview: Sport climb on Megadike North.

current.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: pull over at 1.1 miles beyond the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, at the spot on the left (SE side) where a dirt road joins the pavement, or drive on to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.
current.descent: Two linked pitches to 70 ft total; a 70m rope connects both for a single lower, or lower/rappel each pitch separately with a standard 60m rope.
current.detailed_rack: 3 bolts to wide hangers, then plenty of bolts to a chain anchor on a huge ledge.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted, two pitches; ~20 ft of sustained climbing at the grade near the mini-roofs.
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route at Megadike North (The Dikes, WA). 70m recommended given Megadike North's walls up to ~120ft.

name: Just For Fun
beta: Small holds lead through a little bulge to easier 5.2 ground and the chain anchor.
overview: Easy bolted introduction route off the trail past the break in the Minidike.

current.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. For the Minidike, pull off 1.5 miles beyond the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, on the left (SE) side of the road immediately after the bridge over the river. Cross the road, scramble down the bridge abutment, and follow a trail downstream on the NW side.
current.descent: Lower from the chain anchor on a single strand.
current.detailed_rack: Bolts to anchor chains; standard sport rack.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted.
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route at Minidike (The Dikes, WA). Minidike routes are shorter than Megadike; 60m is sufficient.

name: South Ridge
beta: From the Denny Creek Trailhead, hike the Denny Creek Trail past Keekwulee and Snowshoe Falls to Melakwa Lake, cross talus toward Melakwa Pass (the saddle between Kaleetan and Chair Peak), then follow the scramble trail up the crest of Kaleetan's south ridge to the summit block. The route is mostly a well-worn boot path with a stretch of Class 2-3 scrambling and one short rock-chimney crux near 5,100 ft.
overview: Kaleetan Peak (~6,259-6,260 ft) is a sharp, prominent granite summit above Melakwa Lake in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, about four miles northwest of Snoqualmie Pass in the Cascades' Snoqualmie Pass corridor. "Kaleetan" is Chinook Jargon for "arrow"; the name was given by early Mountaineers club members and formally adopted by the U.S. Board on Geographic Names in 1916. Sidney V. Bryant made the first recorded ascent in 1914, and the standard South Ridge remains a popular Class 3 scramble prized for its accessibility from Seattle and views across the Snoqualmie Pass peaks (Chair Peak, Bryant Peak, Snoqualmie Mountain) and into the Alpine Lakes high country.

current.approach: Start at the Denny Creek Trailhead (~2,280 ft), reached via Forest Road 58 (Denny Creek Road) off I-90 Exit 47. From the trailhead, follow Denny Creek Trail #1014 north/east up the valley. At roughly 1.2-1.3 miles the trail crosses Denny Creek at the 'Slippery Slab' — smooth cascading bedrock and pools that are the last easy, reliable water source before the climb steepens. Beyond the slab the trail climbs through forest, crosses talus/boulder slopes, and switchbacks up to Hemlock Pass (~3.8 miles, ~4,600 ft), where it meets the Melakwa Lake Trail #1011 junction (the right/east fork continues toward Lower Tuscohatchie Lake). Bear toward Melakwa Lake and descend gently about half a mile to the lake basin (~4.3-4.5 miles, ~4,550 ft) below Chair and Kaleetan Peaks — good campsites and the last dependable water before the summit push. From the lake outlet, leave the maintained trail and follow a well-defined but unmaintained climbers' path that heads steeply northwest, gaining Kaleetan Knoll (Peak 5,700) through subalpine trees, heather, and talus. From the knoll the boot path drops several hundred feet down its west side into a rocky, west-facing talus bowl below the saddle that separates Peak 5,700 from Kaleetan's south ridge; cairns mark the crossing but route-finding can be tricky in cloud or early-season snow. Regain the ridge at the saddle and follow the boot path north, just below/along the crest, for a few hundred yards to the base of an obvious gully/ledge system splitting Kaleetan's south face — this is the standard finish, roughly 400-600 vertical feet of Class 2-3 scrambling on loose, exfoliating rock, exiting onto a short summit ridge with one more brief scramble to the true summit (6,259-6,260 ft). One-way distance from the trailhead to the summit is about 9-10 km (matching the 19.3 km round trip) with about 4,500 ft of total gain. Key hazards: the summit gully and upper shoulder hold snow well into early summer — recent parties often describe needing an ice axe and light crampons on the northwest-facing finish into June/July; the rock on the upper peak is loose throughout, and exposure increases near the top; and the talus traverse below the Kaleetan Knoll saddle has no continuous trail, so cairn-following and route-finding judgment (especially in poor visibility) are required.
approach_variant_names: Denny Creek to Melakwa Lake and the south ridge
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line — the standard South Ridge route is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling. Downclimb the summit gully/ledge system carefully; loose, exfoliating rock is the primary hazard on the way down, so descend one climber at a time through the gully to avoid knocking rock onto partners below. From the base of the gully, regain the saddle, re-cross the west-facing talus bowl below Peak 5,700 (following cairns), go back up and over Kaleetan Knoll, and drop down to Melakwa Lake. From the lake, follow Melakwa Lake Trail #1011 back up and over Hemlock Pass, then down Denny Creek Trail #1014 to the trailhead. In early-season conditions, when the gully still holds snow, parties often downclimb facing in or plunge-step an adjacent snow tongue with an ice axe rather than downclimb bare rock; a short hand-line or sling-and-rappel off a natural horn/block is occasionally improvised by parties uncomfortable with the exposed, loose downclimb, but this is not standard practice and there is no documented fixed or bolted rappel anchor on this route.
current.detailed_rack: No rock rack is needed - this is an unroped Class 3 scramble.
current.pro_needs: None required in normal dry summer conditions; not a roped-protection route.
bivy: Melakwa Lake and Upper Melakwa Lake designated sites
current.rope_note: Class 2-3 scramble via Denny Creek/Melakwa Lake; one eroded ~5ft rock chimney near 5100ft requiring 2-3 downclimb moves. No rope standard.

name: North Face
beta: A solid, short alpine rock route consisting of three pitches on granite with excellent anchor systems. The route is mostly low 5th class climbing with sound rock quality throughout most of the climb, though the first pitch contains some loose material. Multiple fixed anchors and bolts make the route straightforward and relatively safe for well-executed rock climbing skills. The climb features excellent views of Liberty Bell and the surrounding North Cascades.
overview: The North Face is the classic, most popular line on Kangaroo Temple (7,572 ft), a detached granite tower on the SE ridge of Wallaby Peak on Kangaroo Ridge above Washington Pass. It's a short (3 required pitches, plus an optional 4th to the true summit block), low-5th-class alpine rock climb on excellent granite, widely used as an introductory multi-pitch/alpine outing (e.g. Mountaineers Basic Rock/Basic Alpine climbs) despite real exposure on the upper pitches.

current.approach: Start from the Hairpin turnout on SR-20 (elev. ~5,150 ft), about 1 mile east of/beyond Washington Pass on the North Cascades Highway. From the large pullout, pick up the climber's trail that switchbacks up into the valley to the southeast — it's faint and boulder-hopping at first through talus and sandy gullies (look for cairns; the tread firms up after the first quarter mile), passing a small dried-up tarn. Stay along the right-hand (west) edge of the timber as you gain the valley headwall. This climber's path/trail gains roughly 1,500 ft over about 1.5 miles to Kangaroo Pass, a broad, view-filled saddle that's the key approach landmark (budget 1–1.5 hrs from the car at a moderate pace; there is no reliable water along this stretch, so carry what you need from the trailhead). From Kangaroo Pass, do not drop straight down the far side — instead contour/traverse south along the base of the slabs descending from Wallaby Peak, losing about 20 ft below the level of the pass, to pick up a good, well-cairned climber's trail. Follow this trail close beneath the slabs, staying below all the major slab bands, traversing toward Kangaroo Temple until you reach a gully system leading up to the high notch at the base of the North Face (about 200 ft below the notch an obvious bench/trail also splits off right toward the Northwest Face for parties headed there instead). Ascend the gully to the notch, which is the start of the North Face route. Hazards are mostly route-finding (the boulder-field tread disappears and reappears repeatedly before the pass) plus loose talus/scree underfoot and, early season, potential snow/ice in the approach gully warranting an ice axe. Total car-to-base time is typically 1.5–2.5 hours; guided/club trip reports cite 7–8 hours car-to-summit-and-back for the full outing.
approach_variant_names: The Hairpin turnout, the boulder-field path to Kangaroo Pass, then the traverse below Wallaby's slabs to the high notch
current.descent: Descend by rappel back down the North Face line to the notch, then reverse the approach trail to the Hairpin. From the summit, the standard descent is three single-rope rappels using a 60 m rope: rap 1 from chain anchors at the top of the North Face; rap 2 from a second set of chains (or, per some trip reports, an alternate flake-and-tree anchor roughly 30 ft below/near those chains) — note a 50 m rope only just barely reaches this station, so a 60 m rope is strongly preferred; the descent line goes over a sharp lip onto vertical face, so manage rope-pull and stance carefully. Rap 3 from the next station lands you on down-climbable low-5th/4th-class terrain just above the high notch where the route began — from there it's an easy scramble/walk back down into the notch and gully. The stations are fixed, but their rigging varies (chains at some, bolts with slung cord at others), so inspect each one before loading; no anchor building should be needed. Once back at the notch, reverse the approach: descend the gully, pick up the climber's trail along the base of the slabs back to Kangaroo Pass, then follow the boulder-field/forest climber's trail down to the Hairpin trailhead. Watch for other parties queued at the rap stations — this is a popular Mountaineers/club route and backups at the anchors are common on weekends.
current.detailed_rack: A standard alpine rack with cams to 3 inches; long slings help reduce rope drag on the broken first pitch.
current.pro_needs: Single rack to 3"; a single 60 m rope is sufficient for both climbing and the descent raps.

name: Southwest Gully
beta: From a high camp in Mesahchie Basin (~6,600 ft), climbers ascend northwest to gain the Katsuk-Mesahchie col area, then work up scree/talus and short rock steps to a bench around 7,400 ft (the last ~100 ft is Class 4). Above the bench, several ribs and gullies lead up through mixed scree, heather, and solid rock; the standard finish follows a leftward-trending gully whose lower half is hidden behind a buttress and which tops out just below the summit's "mushroom" block. In early season (before roughly August) this gully can hold continuous steep snow exceeding 45°, requiring an ice axe, crampons, and solid snow-climbing experience; a small moat often opens along the left edge of the snowfield late season. The summit block itself is climbed via a series of blocks on its west side, Class 3. No technical rock climbing or roped pitches are required by late summer, but the terrain is sustained, loose, and route-finding is nontrivial.
overview: Katsuk sits between Mesahchie and Kimtah on Ragged Ridge, on a sub-ridge locally called the Jagged Edge; the Katsuk Glacier clings to its north slopes. The peak has two nearly identical summits (west and east, measured within roughly half a foot of each other in a 2023 GPS survey, with no definitive true summit established) and the standard route ascends a gully on the southwest side with a class 4 crux near the top — the hardest of the four standard Ragged Ridge Bulger scrambles.

current.approach: Start at the Easy Pass Trailhead on SR-20 (milepost ~151, roughly 30 miles east of Newhalem / ~45 miles from Marblemount). Follow Easy Pass Trail (Green Trails Mt. Logan No. 49) 3.5-3.6 miles and about 2,700-3,000 ft of gain to Easy Pass at 6,550 ft — figure 2-3 hours. The trail crosses Granite Creek on a footlog near the start, climbs through about 2 miles of hemlock/silver-fir forest, then breaks into open avalanche meadows and crosses Easy Pass Creek three times before the final push to the pass; steep snow can linger on this upper section well into July and an ice axe is recommended into early summer. From the pass, drop down the North Cascades National Park side to the end of the first switchback, where a faint, easy-to-miss climbers' path breaks off onto Ragged Ridge — this junction is unmarked and is the most commonly botched route-finding point on the whole approach; if you don't spot the boot path, head off-trail toward the ridge anyway. From there, sidehill northwest across scree, talus, grass and blocky terrain at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft along the south side of the ridge (about an hour), crossing one notable waterfall/stream beneath Mesahchie Peak around 6,500 ft on an easy bench — this is the one water crossing of consequence on the traverse and also a reliable water source. Continue to the basin/shoulder at roughly 6,600-6,870 ft just south of the Katsuk-Mesahchie col, known as Ragged Ridge Camp (only two workable flat tent sites; good water draining the basin). An NPS backcountry permit is required to camp here. From camp, gain a further 200-600 ft to a saddle/bench on the ridge descending from Katsuk's west summit — tedious scree with a short stretch of 4th-class scrambling near the top — then locate the leftward-trending Southwest Gully high on the peak, which runs up toward a mushroom-shaped summit block. Low in the gully, bypass a waterfall by staying on its left (west) side on loose, 'kitty-litter' scree (Class 3). In early season (before roughly July) the entire gully holds steep snow to 45 degrees and demands an ice axe, crampons, and solid snow-climbing technique. Given the ~19.3 km round-trip distance, this is realistically an overnight approach (roughly 5 miles and about 3,000 ft to camp) rather than a single-push dayhike for most parties.
approach_variant_names: Ragged Ridge Camp to the waterfall at 7,760 ft
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the Southwest Gully's Class 3 loose scree, staying left/west of the waterfall low in the gully, back to the ridge saddle/bench, then pick your way down scree to Ragged Ridge Camp. From camp, reverse the roughly 6,600-6,800 ft sidehill traverse (crossing back over the stream/waterfall bench beneath Mesahchie Peak) to regain the base of Easy Pass, climb back over the pass, and descend Easy Pass Trail to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb — there is no rappelling on the standard Southwest Gully route; no fixed anchors, bolted stations, or rappel slings are mentioned in any route description or trip report found. The main descent hazards are loose rock and scree underfoot (rockfall risk onto anyone below in the gully or on the ridge traverse), the same route-finding difficulty relocating the faint climbers' trail junction near Easy Pass's first switchback, and, in early season, downclimbing or glissading steep snow in the gully (45+ degrees in spots) which requires an ice axe and good snow skills.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard scramble by late summer. Some parties carry a short handline or a single rope with a few slings and a picket/cordelette for the summit block or any wet/icy sections, though this is not standard on the dry-season line.
current.pro_needs: Most parties scramble unroped; a short rope is reassuring for the class 4 crux and for less-experienced partners.
bivy: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
Basin camp south of Mesahchie Peak
current.rope_note: ~600ft gully of scree/talus with ~100ft of Class 4 scrambling near a 'mushroom' summit block; loose rock bypassing a waterfall low on route. Steep snow can persist into August in the upper gully (ice axe useful). No rope standard for competent parties.

name: Standard Scramble (off the PCT)
beta: The standard line follows the maintained PCT north from the Snoqualmie Pass trailhead for roughly 4.6-5 miles (up to 5.5 mi one-way depending on exact trailhead/summit points used), then breaks off onto a faint, unsigned boot path near 5,200 ft that climbs directly uphill to the ridge and summit. No technical gear is required in summer conditions; it is popular as a long day hike/scramble combo with the nearby Kendall Katwalk viewpoint.
overview: Kendall Peak sits directly above the Kendall Katwalk, a narrow trail blasted into a cliff face on the Pacific Crest Trail roughly 6 miles north of the PCT Northbound trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass. The mountain has four nearly equal sub-summits; the northernmost is the true high point (~5,799 ft) and is the one reached by this standard route. From the summit and the Katwalk below it, views open down into the Gold Creek drainage and across the Alpine Lakes Wilderness toward Red Mountain and the Chikamin/Lemah group.

current.approach: From I-90 Exit 52 (West Snoqualmie Pass), the Pacific Crest Trailhead (PCT northbound) lot sits just off the exit ramp on a short dirt spur (Northwest Forest Pass required; the ~50-car lot fills early on weekends). From the trailhead (~3,000 ft), follow the PCT north through second-growth forest: a first switchback at 0.6 mi (3,230 ft), a switchback pair at 1.5 mi (3,690 ft), and the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary at 2.0 mi (3,830 ft), where the forest opens into talus. The trail eases downhill slightly to the Commonwealth Creek Trail junction at 2.6 mi (3,775 ft) - stay right/straight on the PCT; the left-hand Commonwealth Basin trail is brushy and easy to mistake for the main tread. Two stream crossings near this junction (plus a small waterfall/seasonal creek around 2.25 mi) are the last reliable water and can run high and tricky in early season. Beyond the junction the PCT climbs steadily under Kendall Peak's west flank through open talus and heather (Kendall Gardens, roughly mile 5, best wildflowers in August), then switchbacks directly below the peak (~5.5-6 mi, ~5,100-5,200 ft). Watch here for a large, distinctive stump partially blocking the left side of the trail at about 5,200 ft; roughly 15 feet beyond it, a boot path forks right (east) off the PCT and climbs straight uphill - this is the turnoff for the standard scramble. Leave the PCT and follow this boot path for the final ~400-500 vertical feet to the northernmost (highest) summit; it's steep, loose dirt and scree with occasional hands-on Class 2 moves, similar in character to the summit pitch on nearby Bandera Mountain. There is no water past the Commonwealth Creek crossings, so carry what you need for the upper mountain. Parties who overshoot the stump/bootpath and continue on the PCT to where it crosses the ridge on the east side can alternatively scramble the ridge crest south to the true summit, but that line is Class 3-4 with abundant loose rock and notably more exposed and dangerous than the bootpath - it is not the standard route. Snow can linger in the boot-path gully and on the PCT traverse below Kendall Gardens well into early summer, so check current conditions before a spring trip.
approach_variant_names: PCT north to the stump at 5,200 ft, then the boot path east
current.descent: Descend the same way you climbed: back down the loose dirt-and-talus boot path to the stump on the PCT, then follow the PCT south/back roughly 5.5-6 miles to the Exit 52 trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no technical rappelling anywhere on the standard route (rappels: 0). The boot path is the steepest and loosest stretch of the whole outing - descending it means kicking down through scree and dirt with hands often needed for balance on Class 2 terrain, and parties should space out or downclimb one at a time in its narrower sections to avoid kicking rock onto climbers below. If any snow remains on the boot path or on the PCT traverse near Kendall Gardens (which drops off steeply to the west), carry an ice axe and know how to self-arrest - a slip or postholing misstep on that exposed traverse is reportedly genuinely dangerous. Do not improvise a shortcut off the ridge or peak's other gullies to save time: parties who left the established bootpath/PCT line have run into unexpected rock bands, avalanche chutes, and difficult creek crossings trying to find a more direct descent. Stick to the boot path and PCT both up and down.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack.
current.pro_needs: None.

name: Southwest Slopes / Gully
beta: From a high camp in the basin below Mesahchie Peak, climbers side-hill traverse west along Kimtah's south face at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft, crossing more than a dozen loose ribs and gullies (mostly class 3). A well-known 'red ledge' cuts across the ribs and greatly simplifies the route-finding. Near the 'Grotesque Gendarmes,' the standard line downclimbs about 150 ft down a buttress and threads a narrow, exposed class 4 gully to bypass a cliff band, then regains the traverse. A final broad, solid-granite gully (class 3) leads up to the ridge just west of the true summit, finishing with a short class 3 scramble across a scree saddle between the west and east (true, 8,649 ft) summits.
overview: Kimtah is the third from the east of the four standard Ragged Ridge Bulgers — Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah, and Cosho, east to west — all included on Washington's Bulger List of the state's 100 highest peaks. It sits above the Kimtah Glacier on its northwest slopes and the Katsuk Glacier to the northeast, in the rugged, trail-less Ragged Ridge massif of North Cascades National Park. Because the peak lies outside LiDAR survey coverage, some listings still give its elevation only as a contour-based estimate of "8,600+ ft."

current.approach: Start at the Easy Pass Trailhead on the south side of SR 20 (milepost ~151, elev. ~3,800 ft). Follow the Easy Pass Trail — a well-graded but relentless climb through old-growth forest and switchbacks along Easy Creek — for about 3.5-3.6 miles and roughly 2,800 ft of gain to Easy Pass itself (~6,550 ft), where the trail crests into open meadows with the first views of Fisher Basin and the Ragged Ridge crest. Do not descend the trail's switchbacks toward Fisher Creek on the far side; instead leave the maintained trail near the pass and begin a cross-country sidehill traverse west along the south side of the ridge, roughly holding the 6,600-6,700 ft contour. This stretch crosses several small gullies and minor buttresses on talus and heather benches, passes below a large basin under Mesahchie Col, and continues west for about another mile. Watch for a waterfall and a band of steep scree partway along that forces a ~200 ft descent to find a safe crossing point — this is the trickiest route-finding section of the approach and is easy to get cliffed out on if you traverse too high. The standard camp is a basin at ~6,600 ft south of Mesahchie Peak, roughly 5 hours and 5-6 miles of travel from the trailhead, with reliable water from snowmelt streams and the waterfall drainage nearby (water can dry up late season). From camp, gain about 800 ft to a bench around 7,400 ft and traverse west along that bench for roughly 2.5 hours toward the Kimtah/Thieves Peak col (~7,900 ft) and beyond, crossing broken granite and slate terrain the whole way — this is sustained, exposed, trail-less cross-country travel, not a simple hike, and route-finding skill at class 3-4 is essential. No reliable water past the basin camp in late season.
approach_variant_names: Ragged Ridge Camp and the red ledge
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the summit gully back to the ~7,400 ft bench, then work back east along the south-slope traverse, staying on or near the outbound line (cairns mark the route in places) to bypass the Grotesque Gendarmes buttress (a short 4th-class downclimb with real exposure) before regaining the sidehill traverse back toward Easy Pass and the maintained trail. This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no fixed rappel stations reported — one winter party downclimbed rather than rappelled because the upper mountain offered no obvious solid anchors, consistent with the loose/fractured granite and slate character of the terrain. A rope, a few slings, and gear for natural anchors (horns, chockstones) are worth carrying as a contingency for a short rappel around the gendarmes or a wet/icy gully, but the standard descent for this route is downclimbing, not rappelling. Main hazards: loose rock and 4th-class exposure at the gendarme bypass, potential snow/runout in the gully early season, and the same tricky waterfall/scree crossing on the return traverse that made the approach route-finding nontrivial — down-climbing steep scree in this section in worsening light or weather is the most commonly cited crux of the whole outing.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard scramble; most parties climb it entirely unroped. A short rope and a few slings/small rack can be carried as a safety option for less-experienced climbers on the ~150 ft class 4 buttress downclimb/bypass near the Grotesque Gendarmes, but it is rarely deployed in summer conditions.
current.pro_needs: Usually scrambled unroped; carry a short rope for the exposed class 3-4 sections if the party wants a belay.
bivy: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
current.rope_note: Class 3-4 cross-country scramble via Ragged Ridge (typically approached from Easy Pass); route crosses a ledge past 'Grotesque Gendarmes,' a cliffy/cave section, then gullies to the summit. No rope standard but route-finding and Class 4 skill required.

name: King Kong - Gorillas Direct Direct
beta: Grade: IV 5.11+ alpine rock climb (5.12a on some topos). Route length: 900 feet (8 pitches) on West Face Wall. First free ascent: September 9, 2016, by Sol Wertkin with Jon Gleason. Route climbs first 4 pitches of Gorillas in the Mist, moves left onto Gorillas Direct (2 pitches), then climbs 2-pitch direct finish up aesthetic splitter crack on overhanging headwall (5.11d-5.12a crux). Connector pitch (5.10b): roof bulge, stem-box, runout overhanging jug climbing. Headwall pitch (5.11d-5.12a): slabby steps, vertical features, meaty hand/fist jams, wild layback sequences. Required gear: double rack cams/nuts (small-medium), two fixed nuts at headwall top. Best season: late summer through early September (before fall storms and snow). Hazards: significant runouts between protection placements, loose rock with hidden chock stones, 30+ meters of overhanging exposure on headwall, alpine weather exposure risk (unplanned bivy possible).
overview: The hardest currently-documented free route on Mount Stuart: begins on the original four pitches of Gorillas in the Mist, cuts left on a ledge system, joins two pitches of Gorillas Direct, then finishes independently with a two-pitch direct headwall finish up a striking splitter crack ('Empire State Building', 5.11d-5.12a).

current.approach: From the Esmeralda/Lake Ingalls Trailhead at the end of FS-9737, hike the Ingalls Way Trail up switchbacks past several waterfalls over Ingalls Pass (about 6,500 ft, roughly mile 3), then continue past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, follow the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge, and contour northwest to Goat Pass (7,600 ft). The West Face Wall, home to the Gorillas routes (Gorillas in the Mist / Gorillas Direct / King Kong), sits in the amphitheater roughly midway between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass. Camping is common near Goat Pass or down at Ingalls Creek.
approach_variant_names: Ingalls Lake to the West Face Wall — same base as the other two lines on the wall
current.descent: Follow the West Ridge to the summit, or descend the main W Ridge gully via scrambling/downclimbing, breaking skier's right onto a large bench, single-rope rappel from a fixed anchor, then downclimb to Stuart Pass bivy sites.
current.detailed_rack: Standard alpine trad rack: single blue alien/purple TCU, doubles from green alien to #2, single #3, single #4, one set of nuts.
rack: Alpine trad rack: single blue alien/purple TCU
Doubles from green alien to #2 cam
current.pro_needs: Sparse protection reported on some traversing sections (notably P6); solid gear on the crack pitches.
bivy: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
current.rope_note: Climbs first 4 pitches of Gorillas in the Mist, cuts into 2 pitches of Gorillas Direct, then 2 pitches of direct splitter headwall finish. Three pitches run ~55m, making 70m more comfortable than 60m.

name: North Ridge
beta: From the 7,900-ft Klawatti-Austera Col (an easy side-trip from Klawatti Col), gain the lower part of the north ridge — easiest on its east side — and scramble Class 3 terrain to a rock tower nicknamed 'The Smokestack' (roughly 8,400 ft). Circumnavigate the Smokestack on its west side via a short gully to regain the ridge crest, then follow the crest to the summit. About 1 hour from the Klawatti-Austera Col, up to 2 hours from the main Klawatti Col.
overview: A Class 3 scramble along Klawatti's north ridge from the Klawatti-Austera Col, working around a rock tower nicknamed 'The Smokestack' before finishing on the summit crest.

current.approach: From Marblemount on WA-20, drive the Cascade River Road (FR-15) about 19-21 miles (paved to roughly mile 10, then gravel/washboard) to the Eldorado trailhead (~2,150 ft). Cross the North Fork Cascade River and follow the unmaintained Eldorado climbers' trail through forest and a boulder field to treeline, then to Eldorado Basin/Roush Creek camps (~6,000-6,300 ft). Ascend the Eldorado Glacier snow dome to the ~7,500-ft notch on Eldorado's lower East Ridge, traverse ~1.5 miles north across the upper Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col (7,800 ft), then continue easily to the nearby Klawatti-Austera Col (7,900 ft) to start the ridge.
approach_variant_names: One col further: Klawatti Col to the Klawatti-Austera col, then the crest
current.descent: Downclimb the ridge crest back around The Smokestack via its west-side gully, return to the Klawatti-Austera Col, then to Klawatti Col. From there re-cross the Inspiration Glacier to the notch on Eldorado's East Ridge, descend the Eldorado Glacier, and follow the climbers' trail to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Typically climbed unroped as a scramble; a rope and a few slings/small cams can be carried for confidence on the exposed knife-edge sections and the Smokestack bypass gully.
bivy: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road

name: Southeast Face / Klawatti Glacier
beta: Grade III alpine route requiring mixed climbing technique. Approach via Klawatti Glacier from the west with one short Class 4-5 rock step over the bergschrund followed by several hundred feet of 40-55 degree snow. Crampons, ice axe, pickets, 60m rope, and single rack to 2 inch are essential. Allow 1-2 hours for climbing depending on amount of roped climbing.
overview: Klawatti Peak is a nunatak — an ice-surrounded rock summit — ringed by the Klawatti Glacier (east), McAllister Glacier (northwest), and Inspiration Glacier (south) in the North Cascades National Park high country. First climbed in 1940 by Lloyd Anderson, Karl Boyer, and Tom Gorton, it lies between Eldorado Peak and Austera Peak/Dorado Needle and is reached only after a full day or more of committing glacier travel. The Southeast Face route climbs directly off the Klawatti Glacier, crossing a bergschrund/moat that is the technical crux before a final snow or short rock pitch gains the corniced summit.

current.approach: From the Eldorado Trailhead on Cascade River Road (large gravel pullout at roughly mile 19, elev. ~2,100 ft), the hike begins by crossing the Cascade River on a log crossing — the exact log/spot shifts year to year and sometimes washes out, so scout up- and downstream if the reported crossing is gone. From the river, pick up the unmaintained but well-beaten Eldorado Creek climbers' path, which switchbacks steeply through timber and brush, gaining about 1,500 ft to a talus/boulder field around 4,000 ft. Stay climbers'-right through the boulders (cairn lines that trend left lead into cliffier terrain). Above the boulder field, a climbers' trail follows a rib up to a basin around 5,500-5,800 ft, from which you descend slightly into the Roush Creek drainage — the last reliable running water on the approach — before re-ascending to bivy sites around 6,100-6,400 ft at the toe of the Eldorado Glacier. From camp, rope up for glacier travel: climb the Eldorado Glacier (crevasses present, worse late-season), then make the long, mostly-flat traverse east across the Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col (~7,800 ft), a broad saddle with good bivy sites on Klawatti Peak's south side. This ice-cap traverse is the navigational crux of the approach — whiteout is common, so carry a map/GPS track and be ready to navigate blind. From Klawatti Col, a short direct climb up the peak's south-facing flank reaches the base of the technical route (the bergschrund and short rock step). Figure roughly 7-8 miles and 6,500+ ft of gain one-way from trailhead to the base of the climb; most parties treat this as a 2-3 day trip with a glacier camp rather than a car-to-car push.
approach_variant_names: Klawatti Col and the south flank to the bergschrund below the face
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line back down to Klawatti Col rather than continuing over the top on a different line. From the summit, downclimb the moderate 40-55° snow/ice slope back to the top of the short low-5th-class rock step that clears the bergschrund near the route's base. Multiple trip reports (including a 'white-knuckle' late-day retreat in worsening weather) describe this step being rappelled rather than downclimbed once the schrund has opened up, which is the norm by mid-to-late season. Expect one rappel of roughly 30m to get past the bergschrund and back onto the glacier — a doubled 60m rope is sufficient; no second rappel is typically needed. Anchors here are natural, not bolted: slung horns, chockstones, or a picket/deadman in snow, so carry a few slings/nuts and inspect any existing tat before weighting it. Below the schrund, re-cross the Inspiration Glacier roped up (same crevasse hazard as the approach, and the spot where fog/whiteout has caught parties off guard right at the summit) back to Klawatti Col, then reverse the Eldorado Glacier, Roush Creek basin, boulder field, and climbers' trail back to the Cascade River crossing and trailhead. The biggest descent hazard on this route is deteriorating weather/visibility on the open ice cap, not the rock step itself — parties should have a bearing or GPS track for the col-to-glacier-camp leg before committing to the climb.
current.detailed_rack: Single rack of small-to-mid cams (~0.3–1 in) and a few stoppers, 2–3 slings, one or two snow pickets for glacier anchors, and a 60m rope (enough for the single rappel).
current.pro_needs: Minimal — a few small cams and nuts to protect the short low-5th step over the bergschrund is normally enough. This is fundamentally a snow/glacier route, not a sustained rock climb.
bivy: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
Eldorado ice-cap / Inspiration Glacier high camp

name: Koala Krack
beta: Climbers finishing the summit scramble use this short pitch to reach the fixed rappel anchors. Start on the slab to the right of the crack, traverse onto it, then climb the wide, left-trending crack to a small sandy flat, and traverse left toward a cairn marking the bolted rap station.
overview: A short, wide diagonal crack on the summit block that links the standard summit-scramble terrain to the bolted rappel station used to descend Kangaroo Temple.

current.approach: The Temple (Kangaroo Temple, on Kangaroo Ridge) is reached from the large pullout at the hairpin turns on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass — the same parking area used for the neighboring Hairpin Crags/Spire Gully climbs. From the pullout, a climber's trail heads south across a boulder field, through forest and more talus (faint, intermittently cairned) up to Kangaroo Pass, about 1 hour. From the pass, an intermittent trail traverses to a gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger; ascending or descending that gully reaches the base of the North Face, Northwest Face, or Southwest Face routes, roughly another hour. Total trailhead-to-summit time runs about 7-8 hours round trip.
approach_variant_names: Hairpin pullout, Kangaroo Pass and the Temple-Little Finger gully
current.descent: From the top of Koala Krack, traverse left to the cairn marking a two-bolt rappel station on the ridge edge; rappel from there and join the peak's standard multi-rappel descent line back toward the notch and Kangaroo Pass.
current.detailed_rack: Gear to 5 inches — a single set of cams covers the wide diagonal crack adequately for this short pitch.
current.pro_needs: Protects well with large cams in the wide crack; very short pitch overall.
bivy: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
current.rope_note: Short, easy single-pitch granite route on Kangaroo Temple's summit block. No dedicated route-specific beta found; inferred from the comparable, slightly harder North Face (5.6, 3 pitches, standard rack to 3in, chain-rappel descent) on the same formation.

name: Standard Route
beta: Kololo Peaks presents three viable multi-day approaches, all exceeding 12 miles and typically requiring 2-3 days with glacier travel. The standard route from the west via North Fork Sauk Trail offers the most established access, climbing through old-growth forest to the Pacific Crest Trail at White Pass, then traversing multiple glacier systems. The climb itself is straightforward Class 2-3 scrambling on talus and snow, with the primary challenge being glacier crevasse navigation and length of approach rather than technical difficulty. Neither summit presents hard climbing; the route involves walking across easy terrain between the west summit and the slightly higher east summit (8,240 ft, the true high point).
overview: Kololo Peaks is a sprawling, multi-summit massif on the southern flank of the Glacier Peak (DaKobed) massif, about 3 miles south of Glacier Peak itself. It has been called 'almost a nunatak' because it is nearly surrounded by ice - the White Chuck and Suiattle Glaciers flank it to the west/north and the Honeycomb and White River Glaciers to the east/south. It's a Class 2-3 snow/glacier objective, not technically hard, but the combination of a 12+ mile approach (much of it off-trail), extensive glacier travel, and remote route-finding make it a serious undertaking reserved for parties with solid glacier-travel and navigation skills.

current.approach: The standard approach follows the North Fork Sauk River Trail (USFS Trail #649) from the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (~2,050 ft), reached via Forest Road 49 off the Mountain Loop Highway south of Darrington. The trail climbs gently through old-growth forest along the river valley for about 5.5 miles to Mackinaw Shelter — a possible camp, though tight for a larger party — crossing several tributaries en route, including Red Creek, which parties describe as interesting but not difficult to ford in normal flow (a trekking pole/sturdy stick helps with balance); it can run considerably higher during spring snowmelt or after rain. Past the shelter the trail turns uphill in earnest, climbing roughly 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks through subalpine forest to a junction with the Pacific Crest Trail in a meadow (~6,000 ft) with the first real views of Glacier Peak and the White Chuck/Kololo massif. Turn right (north) on the PCT and follow it about a quarter mile to White Pass (5,900 ft) — roughly 9 miles and 4,800+ ft of gain from the trailhead, and the last reliable, easy water source before the high traverse. From White Pass the maintained trail ends and the route becomes a boot path: traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin / White River Meadows (~6,300-6,500 ft), the common base camp, either via Red Pass (1.2 miles from the PCT junction) or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck River basin (the 'Foam Pass' variant). From camp, climb to Foam Pass and cross the White Chuck Glacier and Glacier Gap onto the White River Glacier — this is glacier travel, and rope/crampons/axe are standard gear here; crevasses are typically open and visible to weave around by late summer but can be harder to read under early-season snow bridges. From the gap, drop a short way onto the White River Glacier and come at the peak from the south, climbing the snow headwall to the summit ridge and an easy talus-and-ledge scramble to the summit (Class 2+). This is a long approach in its own right — the round trip runs roughly 28-30 miles — so almost all parties camp at White River Meadows or Foam Basin rather than attempting the trailhead-to-summit push in a single push. There are two long approaches: this North Fork Sauk line, and the alternate White River Trail approach from the east, which reaches a similar high basin by a comparably long trail-plus-cross-country line. In mid-July the stretch past White Pass to the high camp near 6,600 ft has several unexpected dips and re-climbs of a couple hundred feet, adding time to the day.
approach_variant_names: North Fork Sauk Trail #649 to White Pass, then the Foam Basin traverse and the White Chuck Glacier
White River trail from the east
current.descent: Descent reverses the ascent line rather than following a separate down-route: downclimb the summit talus/ledges and the snow headwall, and re-cross the White River Glacier, Glacier Gap, and White Chuck Glacier back to Foam Basin/White River Meadows camp, then retrace the boot path over White Pass to the PCT/North Fork Sauk Trail junction and down the switchbacks and river-valley trail miles to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling — no fixed anchors, bolts, or rappel stations are known on this route, and parties describe reversing the glacier-and-ridge line rather than any rope-lowering. The real descent hazards are glacier hazards, not rock hazards: one party found fully open crevasses low on the White Chuck Glacier requiring careful route-finding/crampon work, and a roughly 200-yard section of exposed blue ice (a shallow icefall) on the White River Glacier that demands careful crampon travel; stay roped for glacier travel on the way down as well as up, and expect snow bridges to be less trustworthy and crevasses less obvious in early season than by late summer. Budget real time for the descent — the same party took about 5.3 hours from summit back to camp alone, before the multi-hour trail hike-out. Glissading may be feasible on snow-filled sections for parties comfortable self-arresting, especially early season, but it is an optional shortcut, not a required part of the route.
current.detailed_rack: 30m+ glacier travel rope, and locking carabiners for crevasse rescue.
current.pro_needs: Glacier/snow protection where present; minimal rock pro
bivy: White Chuck Glacier basin, under Kololo Peaks
Sloan Creek Campground and the North Fork Sauk road end

name: Northeast Ridge
beta: An enjoyable alpine route, and the most direct of the three approaches to Kyes. From the northeast base of the peak (~6,000 ft), Class 3 rock along the climber's-left edge of the Pride Glacier leads to the summit via its southeast corner. Glacier travel (crevasses reported) and route-finding through Quartz Basin's cliff bands on the approach add seriousness beyond the rock grade alone.
overview: A more direct historical line up Kyes from the Sauk River (Darrington) side: Quartz Creek Trail to Curry Gap, an up-and-down ridge crossing the Pride Glacier, and a Class 3 rock band to the summit via its southeast corner.

current.approach: From the North Fork Skykomish / Quartz Creek Trailhead at the end of FR 63 (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF, Skykomish Ranger District, via Beckler Road FR 65), follow the Quartz Creek Trail about 4 miles, gaining roughly 1,450 ft, to Curry Gap (~4,000 ft) at the Bald Eagle Mountain Trail junction. From Curry Gap head west/southwest along an up-and-down ridge toward Kyes, leaving the ridge where feasible to cross the Pride Glacier west-northwest toward the cliffs below Monte Cristo Peak, reaching the northeast base of Kyes around 6,000 ft.
approach_variant_names: Quartz Creek Trail over Curry Gap and the Pride Glacier
current.descent: Downclimb the Class 3 rock band back onto the Pride Glacier, re-cross to the ridge, and follow the up-and-down ridge back east to Curry Gap, then descend the Quartz Creek Trail to the trailhead. Ski/snowboard parties have descended the Pride Glacier Headwall's east-facing fall line directly, exiting through forest lower down — a much longer, off-route alternative not recommended for foot travel.
current.detailed_rack: A rope for the Pride Glacier crossing; a light rack/slings for the Class 3 rock band is optional for most parties.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection reported; natural rock/slings if protecting the class 3 band, plus standard crevasse-rescue anchors on the glacier.

name: East Ridge
beta: From a camp at La Bohn Lakes or La Bohn Gap, climbers head west from the gap up boulders and heather onto the east ridge. Parties describe crossing to a false summit just short of the true top, with roughly the final 1/8 mile being a walk along the summit ridge. The line is entirely off-trail Class 2-3 talus with no technical climbing required in summer conditions.
overview: La Bohn Peak (6,585 ft) is a granite summit at the head of Necklace Valley in the eastern Alpine Lakes Wilderness, rising directly west of La Bohn Gap — a broad, tarn-dotted saddle around 5,900 ft between the peak and Mount Hinman (7,492 ft, 1.7 mi east). The standard line follows a climbers' path west from the gap up the ridge and face above La Bohn Lakes, gaining a final ~1,000 ft of Class 2 (occasional Class 3) talus and rock to the summit. It's rarely climbed on its own — most parties tag it as a half-day add-on from a Necklace Valley or Dutch Miller Gap-Williams Lake-Chain Lakes backpack, often paired with Mount Hinman.

current.approach: From the East Fork Foss River Trailhead (~1,650 ft, reached via a signed spur off US 2 near Skykomish), follow the Necklace Valley Trail #1062. The first ~5 miles are easy, gaining only about 600 ft as the trail parallels the East Fork Foss River through old-growth forest, passing established camps and a boot path near mile 4 that drops to the river for water. The trail then crosses the East Fork (log crossing, can be a wet-footed ford or tricky in high water/early season) and turns steep, climbing roughly 2,400 ft in the next 3 miles over large boulders and tree roots on a rugged, minimally maintained tread — the crux of the approach for footing and stamina. This deposits you at Jade Lake (~mile 8, 4,600 ft), the first of the Necklace Valley chain; continue past Emerald Lake (~mile 9, seasonal stream at its north end for water) toward Opal and Cloudy Lakes at the head of the valley under the cliffs of La Bohn Gap, where the maintained trail effectively ends and boot paths fan out. From the Opal Lake camp area, leave the trail and pick up a crude, unmaintained boot path climbing 'La Bohn Creek,' the outlet stream of La Bohn Lakes — a steep, west-facing, often hot and exposed slog with no reliable shade. This path eases at the lowest La Bohn Lake; continue north along the lakeshore/heather benches to the upper lake, then make a short talus/heather traverse east to the broad 5,900-ft saddle of La Bohn Gap (note: USGS maps mislabel the gap roughly 2/3 mile southeast of its true position — verify you're at the correct broad saddle before committing to slopes east of it, which end in a precipitous drop toward Lake Rowena). From the gap, head west up boulders and heather onto the east ridge and follow it, over a false summit and a short, blocky knife-edge, to La Bohn Peak's summit (6,585 ft); stay off the north side of the summit block, which drops away in a cliff. An alternative that avoids losing/regaining elevation is to leave the main trail near Tank Lakes and follow the 'Magic Staircase' — a bench around 5,200–5,400 ft on La Bohn Peak's south side — over to Chain Lakes and then up to La Bohn Gap from the south. Total one-way distance to the summit is roughly 9–10 miles from the trailhead with about 5,000 ft of cumulative gain; this is realistically a 2-3 day backpack for most parties rather than a car-to-car push. Water is reliable along the East Fork Foss and at the Necklace Valley lakes but scarce above La Bohn Lakes.
approach_variant_names: Necklace Valley and La Bohn Creek to the gap
current.descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is involved. Descend the same east ridge and its talus back down to La Bohn Gap, watching footing on loose, occasionally wobbly boulders (parties describe roughly 1,500 ft of piled boulders, some that wobble, on this face). From the gap, reverse the boot path down the steep La Bohn Creek drainage to the La Bohn Lakes and back into Necklace Valley, then rejoin the Necklace Valley Trail #1062 for the long descent back through the boulder/root section to Jade Lake and out along the East Fork Foss River to the trailhead. Parties wanting to avoid re-losing and re-gaining elevation at the gap can instead descend south from the gap to Chain Lakes and take the 'Magic Staircase' bench (~5,200–5,400 ft) back toward Tank Lakes before dropping into Necklace Valley — a reasonable variation but not shorter, mainly smoother underfoot. Key hazards on descent are the same as on ascent in reverse: loose/unstable talus on the peak's flank, potential lingering snow patches on the upper slopes into early summer (which can mask the correct gap location — the true La Bohn Gap is commonly misidentified from the USGS map, and dropping east of the wrong 'gap' leads onto cliffs above Lake Rowena), and the steep, exposed, often-hot boot path down the La Bohn Creek drainage, which is unpleasant and slick if wet. The East Fork Foss River crossing partway down should be treated with the same caution as on the approach.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed for this unroped scramble.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection is used on this Class 2-3 talus scramble; carry an ice axe (and know how to self-arrest) if climbing early season while snow lingers near La Bohn Gap.
bivy: Necklace Valley — Jade, Emerald and Opal Lakes
La Bohn Lakes, La Bohn Gap and the Chain Lakes benches
Money Creek and Miller River campgrounds, Foss River roadhead
current.rope_note: Class 2-3 talus/scree slope approach near Necklace Valley/La Bohn Gap; a couloir ('waterfall route') variant flanks the peak. No technical rope needed under normal summer conditions.

name: Lover's Lane (couloir)
beta: This alpine ice/snow route ascends a north-facing couloir just left (climber's) of the Zipper, with two or three steeper sections requiring ice protection along the way, topping out on a ridge above the Zipper route. From the top, climbers typically rappel 100+ ft (double rope recommended) into the adjacent Zipper couloir, then climb the last of the Zipper and traverse to the summit.
overview: The steepest and narrowest of Lane Peak's three north-face couloirs, climbing sustained 40-60° snow/ice to a notch above and left of the Zipper, then rappelling into the Zipper for the summit finish.

current.approach: Begin at the Narada Falls parking area; travel via snowshoe/ski along the (closed, in winter) Reflection Lakes road, then traverse steep hillsides under Denman Peak toward Lane Peak's base, turning sharply uphill at the first steep avalanche funnel to reach the base of the couloir.
approach_variant_names: Narada Falls, under Denman Peak, and the first steep avalanche funnel
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb to a large tree a few feet below it and rappel from the tree unless the snow is good enough to downclimb. Then plunge-step down moderate slopes toward the Lane–Denman saddle; at the saddle, go to its far left side and descend a steep gully, then retrace the approach. The 100+ ft rappel from the ridge top into the adjacent Zipper couloir (double rope recommended; a 70m rope allows some downclimbing on moderate snow first) is part of the ascent, not the descent.
current.detailed_rack: A 60m rope plus a second rope for the rappel, pickets and ice screws for the sustained 40-60° snow/ice, plus a small rock rack (nuts, small cams, tricams, a few pitons) for the two or three steeper mixed sections; carry a second tool.
current.pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets protect the snow/ice sections; a small selection of nuts, small cams, tricams and pitons backs up the steeper mixed steps, plus gear/slings to rig the rappel into the Zipper.
bivy: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp

name: Last Chance for Gas, AKA Tricky Start
beta: The route's crux is packed into the first ten feet: a technical, pumpy opening sequence that has caused many climbers to fall low. Once past this tricky start, the remaining climbing to the anchor is comparatively reasonable. Photos of the line show technical hooking/mixed-tool sequences, indicating it is regularly dry-tooled as well as rock-climbed.
overview: The bolted line immediately right of The Crack on the Shuksan Crag main wall — a 50 ft sport/top-rope route, 5.11a on rock or M6+ when dry-tooled, named for its tricky, pumpy opening moves.

current.approach: From Bellingham, drive the Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) east through Glacier; continue about 13.3 miles past Glacier to an unpaved turn on the left — Hannegan Pass Road (FS Road 32) — just before the highway crosses the Nooksack River near Milepost 46. Follow Hannegan Pass Road roughly two minutes to a pullout; the crag is the obvious cliff on the left, only a few feet off the road, with this line just right of the prominent crack (Excavation).
approach_variant_names: Hannegan Pass Road pullout
current.descent: Single-pitch sport/top-rope line — lower from the anchor at the top of the route. Because the bolts on this wall (including on this route) are old and rusty, it is recommended to top-rope rather than lead until they are replaced.
current.detailed_rack: Sport draws for the bolted line (though leading is currently discouraged given bolt condition); most parties top-rope using the fixed protection or a rope thrown from above.
current.pro_needs: Bolted sport line, but bolts are old/rusty and not recommended for leading until rebolted — top-rope is the safer current option.

name: Northern Aspect
beta: From a base camp between the two Yang Yang Lakes, the route heads south around a forested ridge and ascends talus to a distinctive 'secret stair' — a precipitous path up compacted dirt and rock through a small gully to a grassy ledge. From there it follows the ridgeline to a rock outcropping beneath Le Conte's North Face, then works around (avoiding) Peak 7004 via east-slope talus and snow before an exposed traverse of narrow, loose ledges gains the summit. Rated class 4 scrambling; a rope, ice axe, and crampons are standard given the glacier travel required just to reach the peak.
overview: The standard route on Le Conte Mountain, an off-trail glacier-and-scramble line reached via the Ptarmigan Traverse: climbers approach from a camp at Yang Yang Lakes, skirt Peak 7004 on its east-slope talus/snow, and finish up an exposed, loose-rock ledge system to the summit.

current.approach: Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount (paved for roughly the first third, then gravel, narrow and steep near the end) 23.1 miles to the Cascade Pass Trailhead (road-end elevation about 3,660 ft). Hike the Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles / 1,700 ft gain to Cascade Pass, then continue cross-country/on climbers' path south on the Ptarmigan Traverse: ascend the Cache Glacier to Cache Col (~6,900 ft), descend to Kool-Aid Lake (~6,100 ft), cross the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier, climb to the Spider-Formidable col (~7,300 ft), and descend to Yang Yang Lakes (~5,800 ft), which serves as the standard base camp below Le Conte's north side. This approach alone is a full day of glacier travel with sustained elevation gain and loss.
approach_variant_names: Yang Yang Lakes, the secret stair, and the outcrop under the north face
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb the exposed ledge traverse and loose rock back to the rock outcropping below the North Face, then descend the east-slope talus and snow to bypass Peak 7004, returning to the Yang Yang Lakes camp. From camp, retrace the Ptarmigan Traverse route: recross the Middle Cascade Glacier, climb back up to Kool-Aid Lake, ascend to Cache Col, and descend the Cache Glacier to Cascade Pass, then hike the maintained Cascade Pass Trail back to the trailhead. Parties commonly camp at Yang Yang Lakes or Pelton Basin/Cascade Pass on the way out rather than exiting in a single push.
current.detailed_rack: A rope is required for the glacier approach; the class-4 summit ledges are typically soloed or protected minimally with a short rope for confidence on exposed steps.
current.pro_needs: Minimal fixed protection is used on the class 4 summit terrain; the technical requirement is glacier travel gear (axe, crampons, rope, crevasse rescue rack) for the approach rather than rock protection.
bivy: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder

name: Leche La Vaca
beta: P1: fun chimney far right on the wall past a small tree, onto a knobby slab with thin corner pro, a spicy 5.8 move left onto another slab, into a corner belay (~30m). P2: fun corner to a flake, move left around it (5.9) into a corner with knobby feet to a large ledge (~30m). P3: left-facing wide lieback corner (#4 Camalot helpful), leave the corner left via delicate face moves to a rampy hand crack, then shorter blocky corners to a large ledge below the roof pitch (~60m). P4: white knobby rock to a small roof with small gear, over the roof and up crack/knobs to a ledge belay (~45m). P5: 4th-class terrain moving up-left toward the summit, steepening to low-5th class near the top — simul-climbing works well; roughly 100m to the summit block.
overview: A 5-pitch, Grade III 5.10a/b trad route established by Tom Ramier, Abe Traven, and Craig Rankin — one of the more moderate multipitch options on the formation.

current.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), hike the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599): gentle forest walking along Mountaineer Creek for 1.5 miles to a log-bridge crossing, then left onto the Colchuck Lake fork at the Lake Stuart Trail junction (about 2.25 miles), then a final boulder-moraine push to the lake outlet — about 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain, 2.5-3 hours. Top off water here, the last reliable source. Continue around toward the lake's south/east shore onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining steep talus and heather to about 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min; a slope that holds wet snow into July and has produced serious slips). Cut climber's-left off the Aasgard trail through a dense slide-alder/heather band (15-20 minutes of real bushwhacking) to the base of the gully system below Colchuck Balanced Rock. Leche La Vaca starts in this same base gully area on the left side of the wall, near Scarface; the final approach scramble to the wall is loose 3rd/4th class terrain. Figure 3.5-4 hours car-to-base overall.
current.descent: Leche La Vaca's fifth pitch, a long 4th-class to low-5th traverse, ends at the summit block — from there it shares Colchuck Balanced Rock's standard walk-off: scramble class 3-4 around the right side of the true summit block (staying off the balanced boulder itself) down to a broad sandy scree/talus gully, descending clockwise back around the peak to the base of the climbs (45 min-1hr). A short step near the top of this descent is sometimes eased with an optional single ~30m rappel off a slung horn (natural anchor) on the east side rather than downclimbing it — treat this as optional, not mandatory. No full rappel of the route itself is required.
current.detailed_rack: Double rack .3–1, single 2, 3, 4 Camalots, and some small widgets (grey Metolius, purple C3, etc.).
current.pro_needs: A #4 Camalot is helpful on the P3 wide lieback corner; otherwise a standard alpine rack covers the route.

name: Lena Lake to Mt Stone traverse
beta: Day 1 follows the well-graded Lena Lake Trail 3 miles to Lena Lake, then a steep, primitive trail up West Fork Lena Creek to Upper Lena Lake (6.5 mi, 4,000 ft gain from the trailhead). Day 2 leaves the trail entirely: climb southwest across meadows/heather toward the ridge south of Mt Lena, follow intermittent way trails west past Scout Lake, over Scout Pass (5,200 ft) and Upper Scout Lake/Scout Basin, over Ullin's Pass (5,000 ft, with views of the 'Ullin's Bathtubs' tarns), then up the steep snow/dirt 'St. Peter's Ramp' to St. Peter's Gate (5,950 ft) — the high point of the traverse and an obvious notch in Mt Stone's SE ridge. Lake of the Angels lies half a mile southwest of the gate in a grassy bowl. The optional Mt Stone summit side-trip climbs a class 3-4 gully on the mountain's south face to a rock bowl, joins the standard west-ridge route, and finishes with a class 2-3 scramble on solid pillow basalt to the summit (about 1,100 ft gain round trip, ~3 hrs). Day 3 descends the Putvin Trail — historic and primitive, with cliff sections (one with a fixed handline, one requiring tree roots) past Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet — to the Putvin Trailhead, about 4 miles by road from the Lena Lake Trailhead where the trip began.
overview: A long, mostly off-trail traverse linking Upper Lena Lake to Mount Stone via St. Peter's Gate, connecting several alpine lakes and basins in the Mount Skokomish Wilderness before finishing on Stone's west ridge. It is usually done as a demanding two- to three-day backpack rather than a technical climb — mostly maintained trail and way-trail, with legitimate scrambling on loose glacial material near the high point.

current.approach: Start at the Lena Lake Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25, ~600-750 ft). Follow the well-maintained Lena Lake Trail (#810) about 3 miles through second-growth and old-growth forest along Lena Creek to Lena Lake (~1,800 ft), a popular backpacking destination with reliable camping and water. Beyond Lena Lake the trail narrows to a steep, primitive tread that climbs the West Fork Lena Creek drainage; continue roughly 3.5 more miles and about 2,700 additional feet to Upper Lena Lake (~4,000 ft total gain, ~6.5 mi from the trailhead), the last reliable water and the last maintained-trail camp before the traverse goes cross-country. From Upper Lena Lake, leave the trail and head southwest/west: pick up the Scout Lake way-trail across meadows and huckleberry-heather slopes past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass (~5,200 ft), descend slightly to Upper Scout Lake, contour high around it into Scout Basin, and climb to Ullin's Pass (~5,000 ft) overlooking the tarns known as "Ullin's Bathtubs." From Ullin's Pass, a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp that angles across a steep hillside below Mt. Stone and ends at a loose, grungy moraine; the final approach to St. Peter's Gate (~5,950 ft, the traverse's high point) is exposed dirt-and-mud slopes with real route-finding demands, about 2.2 miles and 2,200 ft above Upper Lena Lake. This entire off-trail section crosses loose moraine and talus, can hold snow patches well into summer (many parties carry an ice axe), and has no dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the small tarns near Ullin's Pass; fog is common and has caused parties to lose the route. From St. Peter's Gate, most parties descend about 300 ft to the base of a basalt cliff and cache overnight packs there, then follow a vague climber's path up a Class 3-4 gully on Mt. Stone's south face into a rock bowl below the summit block, joining the standard west-ridge route for a final ~100 ft of Class 2-3 scrambling on solid pillow basalt to the true (south) summit.
approach_variant_names: Lena Lake, Upper Lena Lake and the way-trails to St. Peter's Gate
current.descent: From the summit, reverse the west-ridge/south-face scramble line (well-trodden climber's path) back down to the pack cache below St. Peter's Gate — this is the same route used on the ascent, no alternate descent line. From there continue southwest about half a mile to the Lake of the Angels basin, a common second camp, then pick up the primitive, historic Putvin Trail for the exit. The Putvin Trail drops steeply through Whitehorse Basin and past the Pond of the False Prophet; one particularly steep pitch is equipped with a fixed handline rope, and another awkward step is negotiated using a large, exposed tree root as a handhold. The trail continues down to the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road — a different trailhead than the Lena Lake start, roughly 4 miles of forest road away, so plan a car shuttle or a bike stashed at one end to close the loop. The entire route, ascent and descent alike, is a scramble/walk with no technical rock protection or rope work beyond the fixed handline on the Putvin Trail; no rappelling is involved anywhere on this traverse.
current.detailed_rack: No rope typically carried.
current.pro_needs: None beyond an ice axe for occasional steep snow; this is a cross-country/scrambling traverse, not a technical roped climb.
bivy: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
current.rope_note: Short Class 3 section on Mt Stone's west ridge with three ~20 ft downclimbs; some parties want a handline for these. Loose glacial moraine near St. Peter's Gate has a permanent snow/ice field — ice axe recommended.

name: Let it Burn
beta: P1-P2 (5.7, then 5.10c): start as for the West Face up broken ledges, then take the thin-hands splitter on the left. P3 (5.12a, crux): strenuous climbing moves left past 2 bolts, then a splitter to a 2-bolt belay. P4 (5.11a): carry on up the crack system. P5 (5.11c/5.11+): hard, steep moves up the obvious dihedral. P6 (5.11c/5.11+): grab the thin jug flake, move left into a crack and finish with bouldery moves. P7 (5.10a): wander right, then traverse a slab back left. P8-P9 (5.9, 5.8): knobs around the left edge of a roof, then blocky cracks on the crest to the summit ridge.
overview: Let it Burn closely parallels the popular West Face, sharing its approach and first pitch before splitting left up a fairly obvious, sustained thin-crack system. Established by Jens Holsten and Max Hasson at grade IV 5.12a, the crux is a sustained 130-foot 5.12a pitch featuring technical face moves connecting crack systems via 'wild knobs.'

current.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), hike the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) to Colchuck Lake — forest along Mountaineer Creek, a log-bridge crossing at 1.5 miles, left onto the Colchuck Lake fork at the Lake Stuart Trail junction (about 2.25 miles), then a boulder-moraine finish to the outlet (about 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain). Fill water here — it's the last source. Cross the outlet and continue toward the lake's south/east side onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining talus/heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake, then cut left through dense brush to the obvious base gully below Colchuck Balanced Rock. From the gully, scramble up a 3rd-class ramp to the actual base of the technical climbing. A documented approach for this route took about 3 hours 47 minutes trailhead-to-base, matching the 3.5-4 hour estimate.
approach_variant_names: Colchuck Lake outlet into the west cirque
Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, leftmost gully
current.descent: From the top of the route, most parties make an optional ~30m rappel down the south/southwest side off a slung horn (natural anchor, not bolted) — this step can be bypassed entirely if the party avoids the summit block area. After the rappel (or bypass), descend scree or snow rightward (clockwise around the peak) back to the base of the climb. A documented descent took about 50 minutes from the top of the route to the base, plus roughly 3 hours 5 minutes hiking back out to the trailhead. This is the same walk-off shared by the West Face and The Scoop. Loose rock on the scree gully is the main hazard, especially with parties above; watch footing on wet or snow-covered sections early in the season.
current.detailed_rack: Single #1 and #2 Camalot, a single purple TCU/Blue Alien, and doubles from green Alien to #1 Camalot, plus many wires.
current.pro_needs: Doubles in the small-to-mid range plus a good selection of wires cover the sustained crux pitches.

name: East Face
beta: Start on low-angle dihedral left of Lexington-Minuteman gully. Ascend via cracks and chimneys; crux is pitch 5 with exposed traverse. Upper pitches are off-width and chimney climbing. Exit via notch, descend west gully. Standard trad rack essential; doubles to #3 plus a #4, with a single #5 or #6 useful for the short wide sections.
overview: Lexington Tower's East Face is a striking 10-pitch alpine rock climb on the prominent east wall of the Liberty Bell skyline, featuring an exposed no-hands traverse, a crux lieback, and memorable offwidth pitches including one with a jammed 2x4 for pro.

current.approach: Park at the pond pullout on the south side of SR-20, about 1.2 miles east of Washington Pass (a small dirt turnout marked by a roadside pond). The climbers' path starts just left (west) of the highway's east-side guardrail/barrier and immediately begins gaining elevation through forest. It pops out of the trees onto an open scree-and-boulder slope that climbs directly toward the Liberty Bell group towers, with Lexington Tower's east face visible above. Figure 30-45 minutes (some parties report closer to an hour) of steep hiking/scrambling from the pullout to the base of the wall, gaining several hundred feet over roughly a third of a mile. There are two common ways to gain the actual start depending on snow coverage: a gully/snowfield left of the face, or scrambling in from climber's right on rock. Early-to-mid season the approach gully can hold firm snow well into summer (ice axe/traction useful); by late August it is typically dry talus and easily avoided. No reliable water source on this short approach — carry what you need from the car.
approach_variant_names: The hairpin pond pullout, the steep forest path, and the treed ledge below the east face
current.descent: The standard descent is a walk-off, not a rappel-the-face descent. From the notch below the true summit (not the summit itself), head west and downclimb a short gully on skier's left — roughly 20 feet of 3rd-class terrain. Old rap slings are present in this gully but most parties simply downclimb rather than bother rigging a rappel.
