From the base of the gully, traverse right (north) until you intersect the well-worn climbers'/cattle trail that also serves Liberty Bell, and follow it down to join the Blue Lake Trail. Lower down, watch for a faint climbers' path that cuts back toward the highway and saves close to a mile of road-walking versus following Blue Lake Trail all the way to its own trailhead. Some parties instead choose to rappel directly back down the East Face route itself (useful in bad weather or if the walk-off is unfamiliar/snow-covered) — one documented descent of the face took 7 double-rope (60m) rappels, built from a mix of slung horns/rap rings and a couple of fixed/bolted anchors encountered on route. That face-rappel line is not the recommended standard descent, just an alternative to the normal walk-off descent.
current.detailed_rack: A standard rack with gear to 6 inches; a #4 Camalot gets used a lot and a 6-inch piece helps the wide sections, though confident wide-crack climbers can skip it. Two newer bolts protect the offwidth pitch with the jammed 2x4. Bring long runners.
current.pro_needs: Wide-friendly rack; the crux lieback and offwidth pitches reward big gear.

name: Liberty and Injustice for All
beta: About 200 m of climbing with two short 5.12- cruxes on solid edges and thin cracks; two pitches overlap the line of the older aid route Liberty Loop. Cruxes are mostly short boulder problems that lead to good holds, though protection sometimes requires committing above your last piece.
overview: Climbs the East Face about 10m right of Thin Red Line, joining it at Thin Red Line's seventh-pitch anchor. Established in 2014 by Mikey Schaefer, who rope-soloed the line. Technical, well-protected climbing on solid edges and thin crack features, with short bouldery 5.12- cruxes near the start of a couple of pitches leading to progressively easier climbing above — one of the more popular hard free lines on the wall.

current.approach: Same East Face approach as the other Liberty Crack-area routes: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the East Face talus. Liberty and Injustice for All takes a line roughly 10 meters right of Thin Red Line, so locate the correct start among the cluster of East Face lines (it shares some climbing with the old aid route Liberty Loop).
approach_variant_names: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, then about 10 metres right of Thin Red Line
current.descent: Rappel the route with two ropes; the descent is straightforward and every station is a two-bolt anchor with fixed biners. From the top of pitch 5, where the route joins the top of pitch 7 on Thin Red Line, rappel to the pitch-4 anchor and then to pitch 3. From the top of pitch 3, skip the pitch-2 anchor and rappel directly to the pitch-1 anchor, then to the ground: four rappels in all, or two for parties who stop after pitch 3. Alternatively, continue climbing on Thin Red Line from the top of pitch 5.
current.detailed_rack: Mostly bolt-protected with small camming units and a few stoppers for gaps; bring about 14 draws and some long slings, primarily needed on P1.
rack: Single rope (60m); two ropes for rappel from the route (per route beta)
current.pro_needs: Very solid, well-bolted protection overall, though some moves must be committed above the last piece.
current.rope_note: Rappel the route with two ropes from the top of pitch 5; 5 pitches, ~200m/650ft, Grade IV.

name: Freedom or Death
beta: P1 (5.10b/c) climbs a face-and-crack system to bolts on a slab, needing 4-5 gear placements before the first bolt. P2 (5.11c) steps left off the anchor, following rightward-trending bolts with room for a finger-sized piece. P3 (5.12a) follows bolts up and left through sustained, hard-to-aid climbing (bring a .5, .75 and #1 Camalot). P4 (5.11c) starts with an awkward, rough 5.10c traverse left into Liberty Crack; the section above to the anchor is 5.11+ R, though it can feel closer to PG13.
overview: A 4-pitch, fully-bolted-belay East Face line on a leftward-trending ramp right of Liberty Crack, rejoining Liberty Crack just above its P2 anchor; shares its first 3 pitches with A Servant To Liberty.

current.approach: Standard East Face approach; look for the leftward-trending ramp right of Liberty Crack.
approach_variant_names: The hairpin pond pullout and the cairned East Face path, then the leftward-trending ramp just right of Liberty Crack
current.descent: All belays are bolted; the route can be rappelled with a 60 m rope from the top of P3, or parties can continue up the shared terrain into Liberty Crack toward the summit.
current.detailed_rack: A small trad rack supplements the mostly-bolted protection: 4-5 pieces for the unprotected start of P1, a finger-sized piece on P2, and 0.5/0.75/#1 Camalots on P3.
current.pro_needs: Predominantly bolt-protected with all-bolted belays; a small trad rack fills gaps on each pitch.

name: Freedom Rider
beta: Pitches range from 5.6 to 5.11b, with the crux at P3a (5.10d) described as balancey, technical climbing on mediocre gear. Notable features include an offwidth section, sustained hand cracks, Medusa's Roof on P12, and a class-4 scramble finishing the route. No bolted belay stances exist except where the route intersects Liberty Crack.
overview: A long, adventurous 14-pitch East Face outing on often-poor-quality rock with few bolted belay stances, featuring an offwidth section, hand cracks, the notorious 'Medusa's Roof' on P12, and a final 4th-class scramble to the summit.

current.approach: Standard East Face approach; park at the pond pullout near the hairpin turn east of Washington Pass.
approach_variant_names: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, then left along the base to the loose corner system
current.descent: The route finishes with a class 4 scramble to the summit of Liberty Bell, so the way off is the normal summit descent rather than the face. From the top, head east and make a short series of single-rope rappels from fixed anchors (a 60 m rope is enough) into the Liberty-Concord notch. From the notch, descend the Beckey Gully to the Blue Lakes trail on the west side of the mountain, which is the opposite side from the East Face approach, so plan where packs and shoes will wait. Do not rappel the face itself, since apart from the shared stance with Liberty Crack its belays are not bolted.
current.detailed_rack: A standard rack to 3" with extra small nuts and cams, plus cams up to 6" for the crux pitches (including the offwidth section).
current.pro_needs: Mostly natural, sometimes mediocre gear placements; no bolted belays except where the route crosses Liberty Crack.

name: The Independence Route
beta: First climbed wall-style in 1966 by Bertulis and McPherson, freed in 1991 by Steve Risse and Keith Hertel without adding fixed gear (partly yo-yo style over 2 days), and given its first ground-up redpoint in 2009 by Jens Holsten and Max Hasson. Sustained 5.10-5.12 climbing through named features like the Baer Ceiling, Cascade Ceilings, and Well Hung Ceiling.
overview: One of Liberty Bell's three historic 1960s east-face aid lines (with Liberty Crack and Thin Red Line). Established in May 1966 by Alex Bertulis and Don McPherson as a 20-lead aid route at F8 A4 using roughly 180 pitons and 5 bolts; the line has since been substantially freed, with a full free ascent around 5.12a. A sustained, historically significant Cascadian rock outing on the same superb Washington Pass granite as its neighbors.

current.approach: This is on the East Face, so — like Liberty Crack — the approach is not from the Blue Lake Trailhead but from a separate pullout on SR-20 at the hairpin curve just east of Washington Pass. Park on the north shoulder near the curve, walk back toward the pass to a small pond on the south side of the highway, round its east end, and follow a cairned boot path north into the forest. The path climbs through timber and breaks out onto the talus field directly below the East Face after roughly an hour. From where the path reaches the talus, continue right (north) along the base past the Liberty Crack starts to the far right-hand end of the face, below the red Baer Ceiling roof about 85 m above. No water source along the way; watch for the cairned track being hard to follow in low light, and loose talus underfoot at the base.
approach_variant_names: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, then all the way right to the north edge of the face
current.descent: The Independence Route is a serious, sustained 12-pitch line (first climbed wall-style with 180 pitons and 5 bolts, later freed at 5.12a/5.11) that tops out on Liberty Bell’s upper mountain, so it funnels into the standard Liberty Bell descent used by other summit-finishing routes. From the summit, downclimb the upper pitch a short way and go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60 m rope reaches a sandy ledge; work right and down to a bolted station, then make two single-rope rappels of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Parties who downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem to the first bolts instead of making the tree rappel do two rappels in all. From the notch, downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers’ path and the Blue Lake Trail. Given the route’s length and serious character, plan for a long day-into-evening descent; loose rock in the notch gully is a real hazard when tired or descending in the dark.
current.detailed_rack: Single to double rack through hand size with a set of nuts; a few small pieces for thinner sections.
current.pro_needs: Standard rack; bring smaller pieces for the thin spots.

name: Overexposure
beta: From the Liberty-Concord notch, either a runout 5.8R left variation (poor pro for ~30 ft) or the original line up the top of the notch ramp reach a shared anchor; pitch 2 climbs up and right to a clean white dihedral to a sloping ledge with chain anchors.
overview: An aptly named, exposed moderate free climb on Liberty Bell's west face. Sustained, technical crack and face climbing on outstanding Washington Pass granite, with the airy position that gives the route its name.

current.approach: Overexposure starts right at the top of the notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower, so the trailhead-to-base approach is identical to the Beckey Route: Blue Lake Trailhead (FS Trail #314) → 1.7 miles of maintained trail to the small meadow/stream crossing → climbers' boot path through slabs, talus, and meadow to the fork below the notch → stay left to the notch itself at ~7,300 ft (about 2 miles, ~2,100 ft gain, 1.5-2.5 hours). Because the route begins above the notch rather than at it, budget a little extra time and care scrambling up into the initial belay compared to Beckey Route parties, and expect the same early-season snow in the approach gully requiring an axe.
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail and the Beckey gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, then scramble above it
current.descent: The route’s 2nd pitch tops out at the same bolted anchor system that starts the standard Liberty Bell descent, so most parties either stop there or continue a few hundred feet of 4th/low-5th-class scrambling to the true summit, then descend the standard way. From the summit, downclimb the upper (4th) pitch about 20 ft to the first ledge, then go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60m rope reaches a flatter area; from the bolted anchor there, one double-rope rappel (or two single-rope rappels if only carrying one rope) reaches the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. From the notch, downclimb the loose approach gully back to the climbers' path and the Blue Lake Trail. All anchors are bolted or fixed tree slings — no natural gear or v-thread anchors are needed. Some parties instead rappel back down the Overexposure line itself, a couple of enjoyable rappels on a mix of bolts and gear or tree anchors, directly into the approach couloir where packs were cached, particularly when the main descent line is congested.
current.detailed_rack: Double rack of small to medium cams plus nuts; bring extra small pieces for thin sections.
current.pro_needs: Emphasis on small protection for the hardest, thinnest pitches.

name: Serpentine Crack
beta: Grade III alpine rock, 5.11 crux. Four pitches on Liberty Bell West Face. Pitch 1 (5.8): Slab moves left into corner with short bulge. Pitch 2 (5.11 crux): Steep, awkward fist crack past the right side of a roof, physical, excellent gear. Pitch 3 (5.10): Left-angling hand crack with roof/bulge exit. Pitch 4 (5.7): Navigate tunnel or harder left slab variation, then simul/scramble on exposed sunny arete to summit. Approach via Beckey Route approach, staying left at fork in gully. Excellent hand crack climbing with minimal traffic. Hazards: loose rock from freeze-thaw cycles, afternoon thunderstorms, exposure on final arete.
overview: A striking, winding crack line on Liberty Bell's west face giving sustained, well-protected crack climbing on excellent Washington Pass granite. A sustained 5.11 outing with a physical, wide crux pitch.

current.approach: From the Blue Lake Trailhead on SR-20 (about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, 5,400 ft), hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.7 miles to the signed Liberty Bell climbers' trail just past a small stream in a meadow. Follow it left up slabs, talus and heather into the gully below the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, as for the Beckey Route. Where the gully forks, stay left and cache packs, then scramble 4th-class ledges up and left to a slung small pine above slabs at the base of the crack on the west face.
current.descent: Serpentine Crack finishes on an exposed, sunny arete with a 5.7 simul-climb or scramble to the true summit, so the descent is the standard one used by all summit-topping Liberty Bell lines. From the summit, downclimb the upper pitch a short way and go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60 m rope reaches a sandy ledge; work right and down to a bolted station, then make two single-rope rappels of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Parties who downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem to the first bolts instead of making the tree rappel do two rappels in all. From the notch, downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers’ path and the Blue Lake Trail.
current.detailed_rack: Single to double rack through hand size with a set of nuts to protect the continuous cracks.
current.pro_needs: Standard crack rack; the line follows protectable crack systems.

name: Thin Red Line
beta: Grade: 5.12 (YDS), Grade IV overall. 11 pitches, approximately 1,100 feet of climbing. Route follows intricate crack systems and faces on East Face of Liberty Bell. Hazards: significant rock fall danger in approach gully (parties above knock rock down it, bowling-alley style); loose rock throughout approach; exposed alpine terrain; weather exposure on big wall. Required skills: advanced alpine rock climbing, 5.11+ crack climbing, self-rescue, anchor building, multi-pitch experience. First ascent: 1967 (aid climbing); free ascent variation established 2008 by Mikey Schaefer. Best season: June-September; July-September strongly preferred (late June requires ice axe, crampons). Notable: route features substantial fixed gear on most pitches; descent via two-rope rappel from M&M Ledge or summit traverse.
overview: A classic sustained crack line up the steep East Face of Liberty Bell at Washington Pass — one of the area's renowned harder free climbs on superb golden granite. First climbed (aid) by Jim Madsen and Kim Schmitz on July 29, 1967; first freed by Kate Rutherford and Mikey Schaefer in September 2008, at 5.12c.

current.approach: From Highway 20 hairpin curve on east side of Washington Pass, locate small pond on south side of road; trailhead pullout on north side of highway; follow climbers' path marked with cairns from pond into forest
approach_variant_names: The hairpin pond pullout and the cairned East Face path, then right of Liberty Crack
current.descent: Two documented options. (1) From the top of the route near M&M Ledge, work climber's left to good bolts and make four double-rope rappels (2 ropes) essentially to the ground at the base of the East Face — this is the faster option and returns you directly to your pack/the East Face approach. (2) If you continue to the true summit instead, descend via the standard Liberty Bell notch route: downclimb east ~100 ft through trees/loose rock to the 2-bolt station, then make two roughly 25m rappels (the second off a bolted anchor) down into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, then hike down the scree/snow gully to the climbers' trail along the base of the west faces — but this leaves you on the opposite (west) side of the mountain from your car at the East Face pullout, requiring a shuttle or road walk back.
current.detailed_rack: Double rack of small to medium cams, a full set of nuts, and extra small pieces for the thin cracks.
current.pro_needs: Emphasis on small cams and nuts for thin, sustained crack protection.

name: Liberty Crack (Free)
beta: Follows Liberty Crack's original aid line but climbed entirely free; pitch 1 (5.11-) leads to the crux pitch 2 'Lithuanian Lip' (5.13b) - a scrunchy, powerful traverse to finger locks above the lip and committing moves to a small stance. A slab variation on pitch 3 (5.12) avoids the original bolt ladder.
overview: A modern free variation to the historic Liberty Crack aid line. Liberty Crack was first freed in 1991 by Brooke Sandahl, who led the crux roof/crack pitch on gear and toproped the protectionless slab beside the old bolt ladder. Mikey Schaefer, Shanjean Lee, Blake Herrington, and Nathan Hadley later established a fully free variation around the bolt ladder (2016-2017): the new Pitch 3 slab moves right before the ladder, clips a higher bolt, crosses sloping ledges and mantels through cruxy foot moves (5.12), then rejoins the original line for the 5.11+ Pitch 4, which has a thin crux below a small roof.

current.approach: Drive to the hairpin turn on WA-20 just east of Washington Pass and park at the pullout on the curve (this is a different trailhead than the Blue Lake TH used for the SW/NW Face routes). Walk back toward the pass and find the small pond on the south side of the highway; a cairned climbers' path leaves from the pond's east end and switchbacks up through forest for roughly a mile, breaking out into a talus field directly beneath Liberty Bell's East Face. From the base of the talus, traverse left (climber's left) on 3rd/4th-class ledges for about 40 ft to reach the start of the crack system. This approach is short (about an hour) but steep in its upper section, with a bit of loose talus underfoot near the top — no water source along the way, so carry what you need.
approach_variant_names: The hairpin pond pullout and the cairned East Face path, then 40 ft left along the base
current.descent: Liberty Crack (Free) tops out at the same alcove/bolted anchor used by the original aid line. From there, work along ledges to a double-bolt rap anchor and make two rappels (about 25 m each, 80-100 ft by different accounts) down into the Beckey Gully — the same rap line used by the standard Liberty Crack and Beckey Route descents — landing near a tree anchor in the gully. From there it's a downclimb/walk down the gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch and back to the climbers' path. All anchors on this line are bolted (shiny modern bolts plus a tree station); a single 60m rope is adequate for a one-day car-to-car push, though some parties opt to downclimb the sheltered Beckey Route slab unroped instead of rapping the last section.
current.detailed_rack: A full big-wall-style free rack from micro cams through #3, with hand-crack sizes (#1-#1.5) as the primary placement range; nuts have limited utility since most placements are cam-only. One backup knifeblade piton for potential aid sections, rarely used on a free ascent.
rack: Cams purple C3 to #3, doubles recommended, extra tips-to-fingers sizes (red C3-0.4)
current.pro_needs: Fixed bolted anchors protect the crux Lithuanian Lip and slab-variation pitches; upper pitches revert to trad gear in a granite crack/corner system.
current.rope_note: 60m sufficient for a 1-day ascent (12 pitches, 1200ft, Grade V). Verify current topo if planning a multi-day rap strategy.

name: Liberty Traverse
beta: Grade V alpine, 5.9 YDS, 26 pitches, approximately 2,000 ft (606 m) of climbing. Route composition: Beckey Route on Liberty Bell (5.3-5.6), North Face of Concord Tower, North Face of Lexington Tower, Northwest Corner of North Early Winter Spire (5.9+), Southwest Rib of South Early Winter Spire. Hazards include significant rockfall danger in the approach gully, which funnels falling rock like a bowling alley, exposed alpine terrain, route finding challenges. Requires excellent trad climbing skills, solid alpine rock climbing experience, and good protection/anchor placement ability. Standard rack with couple bigger pieces for North Early Winter Spire. Short rappel descent from summits. The individual summits, the Beckey Route above all, are busy on summer weekends, though few parties do the full traverse. Best season: July-August during optimal weather windows. Typically done as 1-2 day alpine climb with experienced parties.
overview: The classic Liberty Bell Group traverse: start up the Beckey Route on Liberty Bell, continue over the North Face of Concord Tower and the North Face of Lexington Tower, then the Northwest Corner of North Early Winters Spire and the Southwest Rib of South Early Winters Spire. Roughly 26 pitches total across five summits (two Grade III climbs and three Grade II climbs), graded V/IV 5.9 overall. The short approaches between towers let strong parties link two or more summits in a single long day.

current.approach: South side of Highway 20, 1 mile west of Washington Pass overlook; from trailhead follow Blue Lake Trail 1.5 miles to climber's trail junction
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch (traverse start)
current.descent: This is a link-up, not a single down-route: after topping out Liberty Bell via the Beckey Route, the traverse continues over the North Face of Concord Tower, then the North Face of Lexington Tower, then the NW Corner of North Early Winter Spire, finishing on the SW Rib of South Early Winter Spire — five summits total. Between summits: rappel the south face of Concord to reach Lexington, climb Lexington and rappel its south face, cross a short but exposed 3rd-class section, make one more short rappel, and walk to the base of North Early Winter Spire. After finishing on South Early Winter Spire, descend via that peak's standard South Arête rappel line — bolted chain anchors allow 2-3 single-rope rappels with a 60m rope back down its gully — then hike back to the Blue Lake Trail. Even fast parties spend most of a day on the rock, and car-to-car time with all the transitions and the final descent typically runs 12-14 hours; a light rack, one 60m rope, and comfort simul-climbing/downclimbing 5.9 terrain are standard for parties doing it quickly.
current.detailed_rack: A standard alpine rack suffices for most of the traverse, with doubles from about 2 to 4 inches and a single #5 cam added for the wide cracks on North Early Winter Spire and the Bear Hug on South Early Winter Spire.
rack: Standard alpine rack of cams, plus doubles from about 2 to 4in and a single #5 for the wide pitches on North and South Early Winter Spires
Single 60 m rope; every rappel between towers works as single-rope rappels
current.pro_needs: A standard rack, with doubles to about 4 inches and a single #5 added for the wide pitches on North and South Early Winter Spires.
current.rope_note: Not recorded; inferred standard for the area given the traverse links 5 summits (Liberty Bell Beckey Route + Concord N Face + Lexington N Face + North Early Winter Spire NW Corner + South Early Winter Spire SW Rib), 26 pitches total.

name: Southeast Slopes Scramble
beta: Standard summer/fall line to the summit: trail to Lake Valhalla, then off-trail travel up southeast-facing slopes to a saddle on the southeast ridge and along the ridge to the top. No rope or technical rock gear is needed in dry conditions; the same slopes are also skinned/skied or snowshoed as a separate winter tour when snow-covered.
overview: A roughly 9-mile round trip, off-trail scramble up Lichtenberg Mountain's southeast slopes, gaining about 2,500 ft. No maintained trail reaches the summit: from the Smithbrook Trailhead, climbers follow the Smithbrook Trail and Pacific Crest Trail past Lake Valhalla, then leave the trail near the lake's south end and pick a cross-country line up boulder fields and heather benches to Lichtenberg's southeast ridge, following the ridge to the summit. The summit gives views of Lake Valhalla directly below, plus Glacier Peak, Mount Baker, and (on clear days) Mount Rainier.

current.approach: Park at the Smithbrook Trailhead (elev. ~4,000 ft) on Smithbrook Road (FR 6700), about 3 miles up from Hwy 2. Start on the signed Smithbrook Trail (part of the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness trail system) and climb via nearly 20 short switchbacks, gaining about 650 ft in about a mile to Union Gap on the PCT — Lichtenberg's summit is visible to the south for much of this stretch once the forest opens up. At Union Gap, turn left (south) onto the Pacific Crest Trail and follow it about 2 miles, contouring below Lichtenberg's east flank, to Lake Valhalla (~4,830 ft), passing through a mix of forest and open meadow/heather and crossing Smith Brook along the way (a reliable water source and a good place to filter before leaving the trail). From the north or east shore of Lake Valhalla, leave the PCT and begin the off-trail portion: contour and rising-traverse around the lake toward the peak's south/southwest side, picking through heather benches, boulder fields, and increasingly loose talus. There is no maintained trail above the lake — expect real route-finding, some bushwhacking through scattered subalpine fir, and a few short cliff bands that force minor backtracking; a GPS track or written beta is genuinely useful here. The standard line aims for a prominent gully on the south/southwest side of the summit tower (often snow-filled into early summer — an ice axe and sometimes light traction are worth carrying outside of peak summer), climbed as scree/talus with a bit of low third-class scrambling near the top to gain the final summit block. Total gain from the trailhead is roughly 2,000-2,500 ft over about 9 miles round trip, with 6-7 hours being a typical leisurely round-trip time. On a fine mid-October Saturday the trailhead lot was full soon after 8 am and the overflow parked at wide pullouts a few hundred feet down the road; the Smithbrook trail was very muddy.
approach_variant_names: Smithbrook Trail and the crest trail to Lake Valhalla
Crest trail north from Stevens Pass
current.descent: Descend by the same line used on the ascent: down-climb the summit gully (loose scree/talus, care needed with footing and for parties below you kicking rock), then reverse the traverse around Lake Valhalla's south/east side back to the Pacific Crest Trail. Pick up the PCT northbound, follow it back over Union Gap, and descend the switchbacked Smithbrook Trail to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble route with no rappelling required and no fixed anchors on the mountain — rope and rappel gear are not standard kit for this line. The main descent hazards are the loose, unstable talus and scree in the summit gully (helmet recommended, stagger the group to avoid rockfall onto climbers below) and the off-trail route-finding back down to Lake Valhalla, especially in flat light, fog, or if descending after a winter/early-season ascent when the gully may still hold snow (in which case an ice axe and caution on firm morning snow are warranted). Refilling water is easiest at Lake Valhalla or the Smith Brook crossing on the PCT before the final trail miles out.
current.detailed_rack: None required — this is a non-technical Class 2 walk-up/scramble in dry conditions; no rope or rack is carried.
current.pro_needs: No fixed or removable protection needed; it's a hands-occasionally-on-rock Class 2 scramble, not a roped climb.
current.rope_note: No rope needed; Class 2 non-exposed scramble, 9mi/2500ft gain.

name: Southeast Ridge (from Lichtenwasser Lake)
beta: The ridge is an obvious ski-touring objective in winter. In summer it is a 7-mile, 2,100-foot scramble starting from the first switchback on Smith Brook Road / FR 6700 and following the Lichtenwasser Lake fishing trail to a saddle on the southeast ridge. Jim Brisbine's party climbed it as a rock scramble over 20-21 September 1975, camping at Lichtenwasser Lake and continuing over the true summit to The Lichtenhorn before descending the west ridge. The winter version has you leave the road at the first major hairpin, head southwest up wooded and steep but always snowshoeable hillside, traverse toward Lichtenwasser Lake at about 4,600 ft (crossing the lake if it is frozen), then take easy slopes to the ridge crest and follow the summit ridge to the top. A winter north-side version is given with compass bearings: ski 2.6 miles up Smithbrook Road, leave it before the major switchback near 3,970 ft, follow a true bearing of 177 degrees to Lichtenwasser Lake, then 248 degrees from the lake's south end to a 5,640-foot saddle, and ascend the southeast ridge to the summit — about 5.2-plus miles, rated 2 to 2+ in skill and 2-minus in fitness, and included among the classic backcountry ski and snowboard routes in Washington. Avalanche hazard is the defining concern; both sides of the mountain present it.
overview: The short, direct line on Lichtenberg's northeast side and the peak's most-travelled route: a fishing trail to Lichtenwasser Lake at 4,708 ft, then open slopes southwest to a 5,640-foot saddle and an easy rocky ridge to the 5,844-foot summit. It is a rock scramble in summer and the classic Stevens Pass ski and snowshoe tour in winter.

current.approach: Summer: drive US 2 to the Smith Brook Road / FR 6700 turnoff 3.5 miles east of Stevens Pass and follow the unpaved road up toward the Smithbrook Trailhead. Park at or near the first major switchback and find the Lichtenwasser Lake fishing trail, which leads roughly southeast then south through forest to the lake at 4,708 ft (47.7924, -121.0768). From the south end of the lake leave any semblance of path and climb southwest up open and lightly wooded slopes to the broad 5,640-foot saddle on the mountain's southeast ridge; turn right (northwest) and follow the ridge to the summit. Winter: FR 6700 is unplowed, so park on the shoulder of US 2 at or just before the Smith Brook Road turnoff, around mileposts 68.7-68.9 and 4 miles east of Stevens Pass, and skin or snowshoe 2 to 2.6 miles up the snow-covered road — it is usually well packed by other parties. Leave the road at the first major hairpin (near 3,970 ft), head southwest and then follow a bearing of 177 degrees true to Lichtenwasser Lake, crossing it when frozen, and continue on 248 degrees to the 5,640-foot saddle before finishing up the ridge.
current.descent: The normal descent is a straight reversal: back down the summit ridge southeast to the 5,640-foot saddle, then northeast down the open slopes to Lichtenwasser Lake, and out on the fishing trail to Smith Brook Road. In winter this is the ski descent as well, and it is the reason the route is popular — the north side generally holds better snow through the season than the south. Two variants are known. Brisbine's 1975 party continued west over the true summit to The Lichtenhorn and descended the west ridge, which makes a traverse of the whole massif but commits you to trailless ground on the far side. There is also a circuit going up one side of the mountain and down the other, exiting south toward the Yodelin area near milepost 66.25, 1.3 miles east of Stevens Pass — that exit crosses private land near the lodge and homes, so ask permission before parking there. Whichever you choose, assess snow stability continuously before dropping into any steep slope: both flanks present avalanche hazard, and the south side in particular sheds massive slides from time to time.
current.detailed_rack: No rock gear.
current.pro_needs: None. There is no protectable rock climbing on this route and no fixed anchors anywhere on the mountain.

name: West Face (5.9+ rock route)
beta: James Nakagami climbed the West Face at 5.9+ with Dan 'Danimal' Capellini and a third partner. The wall sits just above Lake Valhalla; the approach is a short walk from the Smithbrook trailhead of about an hour, and it is an easier walk in than Snow Creek Wall. A grand west face is one of the mountain's three distinct routes, and one party was turned around by the sheer wall before reaching the summit by an easier line, which confirms that this is genuine roped terrain rather than a scramble. Beyond the grade, the location and the approach, the beta is thin: no topo, pitch count, rack list or descent description is available. Anyone going should expect to do their own reconnaissance from Lake Valhalla, and plan for a full trad rack and a walk-off.
overview: A roped rock line on the steep west wall that rises directly above Lake Valhalla — the feature known as Lichtenberg's 'grand west face' and the reason parties who try to scramble the peak from this side get turned around by the sheer wall. Reported at 5.9+ and reached in about an hour on foot from the Smithbrook trailhead.

current.approach: Drive US 2 to the Smith Brook Road / FR 6700 turnoff 3.5 miles east of Stevens Pass (31 miles west of Leavenworth) and follow the unpaved road roughly 2.5-3 miles to the Smithbrook Trailhead at about 4,000 ft. Hike Smithbrook Trail #1590 for 0.9 mile to the PCT at Union Gap, turn left (south) onto the PCT #2000 and follow it 1.7 miles over the ridge crest and down toward Lake Valhalla at 4,836 ft — about 3.5 miles and 1,500 ft of gain in total. The west face rises directly above the lake's east shore, roughly 1,000 ft of relief. The 2002 report gives the walk in as about an hour, which implies a fast pace on this trail. Scope the wall from the lake or from the PCT high point on the way in; there is no marked or described start.
current.descent: No descent is described anywhere for this route, which is the single biggest gap in what is known about it. What is known about the mountain's geography suggests the options: from the top of the west face, the southwest slopes lead back down to the outflow of Lake Valhalla at class 2, and the northeast side drops toward Lichtenwasser Lake at 4,708 ft on similarly easy ground — both of these are established walking descents used by the peak's scramble routes. There are no fixed anchors, bolts or rappel stations recorded anywhere on Lichtenberg Mountain, so a party planning to rappel the line should expect to build and leave their own gear. Confirm your descent plan by eye from the lake before you commit to the wall.
current.detailed_rack: Given a 5.9+ grade on an obscure Cascades wall with no recorded fixed gear, a full single rack of cams and nuts, double ropes for a possible retreat, a generous set of slings for blocks and horns, and tat and nuts to leave on a bail anchor would be the conventional preparation.
current.pro_needs: Not documented. No bolts, fixed anchors or rappel stations are recorded anywhere on Lichtenberg Mountain, so assume the route is entirely on natural protection and that any anchor you need, you build.

name: West Face - West Rib (Lichtenhorn / West Peak)
beta: Historic climbing-club parties describe an off-trail approach from the Old Lake Valhalla/Lake Janus trailhead via Union Gap and Lichtenberg Pass, then a rock climb up the west face and west rib of the west peak, with descent down the easier northeast slope back toward the start. Little is known about grade and protection; treat this as an obscure, lightly-traveled line rather than a well-established route.
overview: A little-documented technical rock line up the west face and rib of Lichtenberg's western sub-summit (the ~5,800+ ft 'Lichtenhorn'), the rocky pinnacle overlooking Lake Valhalla, approached via Lichtenberg Pass and descended via the northeast slope.

current.approach: From the Old Lake Valhalla/Lake Janus Trailhead on Smith Brook Road (~4,150 ft), follow the trail toward Union Gap and continue to Lichtenberg Pass, then leave the trail to approach the base of the west face.
approach_variant_names: Smith Brook road trailhead via Union Gap
Crest trail north from Stevens Pass
current.descent: The 1978 party descended the Northeast Slope. From the top of The Lichtenhorn, downclimb the easy blocky ground on the north-east side of the west peak (reversing the class 3 wrap-around past the summit spire first if you climbed the direct finish), then follow open slopes and heather benches northeast and east toward the basin holding Lichtenwasser Lake at 4,708 ft. Pick up the fishing trail at the lake and follow it northeast, then drop to Smith Brook Road / FR 6700 and walk the road back down to the Smithbrook Trailhead. This closes a natural traverse of the mountain and avoids reversing the loose face. The alternative — and the simpler option if the party is unfamiliar with the northeast side — is to reverse the west rib exactly as climbed back to the PCT saddle, then retrace the PCT and Smithbrook Trail. Downclimbing the rib is slower than it looks because the sandy chutes are unpleasant to descend; stay on the blocky crest and on the heather ribs. In either case, expect the descent to take longer than the ascent and start it with daylight in hand: there is no path anywhere on the mountain and it is very easy to end up above cliff bands above Lake Valhalla in poor visibility.
current.detailed_rack: A rack of nuts and small-to-mid cams (~0.3-2in) with 4-6 shoulder slings and a couple of double-length slings covers this rough-granite line, per the documented Lichtenberg Pass approach and northeast-slope descent.
current.pro_needs: Protection is optional on the standard class 3 line and minimal on the direct finish. What gear there is goes into blocky granitic rock and horns rather than clean cracks, so slings are more useful than cams. There are no fixed anchors, no bolts and no rappel stations anywhere on the route — anything you build, you build and leave, or you downclimb.

name: Wilkes-Booth (Northwest Face)
beta: Start on the northwest face just right of the prominent hanging glacier with a 60 m WI4 pitch, the route's crux, shared with Shooting Gallery on neighbouring Assassin Spire; its upper half is overhanging, poorly protected ice of doubtful quality. Above, cross a snowfield and climb a vertical ice curtain and a well-protected step of glacial ice into the upper amphitheater, the basin between Lincoln Peak and Assassin Spire, simul-climbing along its west side. On Lincoln's northwest wall, about four roped pitches of steeper ice follow, with snowfields up to 70° between them; the obvious central flow gives about 120 m of WI3+ in two long pitches. From the upper snowfield, follow a rime-covered ridge to a sub-summit, downclimb a short rime step, and climb a final icy gully to the summit. Descend the southwest face route.
overview: Wilkes-Booth climbs about 2,000 ft of glacial, alpine and water ice on Lincoln Peak's northwest face, with steep snowfields between the ice and a rime-covered ridge to finish. Its first pitch, a 60 m WI4 lead with overhanging, poorly protected ice in its upper half, is the crux and is shared with the lines on Assassin Spire. The route depends on unusually good ice build-up; the first ascent was a single 18.5-hour push from the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead in a one-day March weather window, descending the southwest face.

current.approach: Start at the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead (FS Road 39, Trail #677) near Glacier, WA, and follow the Heliotrope Ridge Trail roughly 2 miles through old-growth forest and several avalanche-chute creek crossings to the flat former Kulshan Cabin site (~4,700 ft). From Heliotrope Ridge, cross the lower Thunder Glacier to the base of Lincoln's northwest face and the prominent hanging glacier, where the route starts at the same point as the routes on Assassin Spire. Rope up for the glacier; the face is big and complex and cannot be seen whole from the approach.
approach_variant_names: Heliotrope Ridge to the Kulshan Cabin site, then onto the Thunder Glacier below the northwest face
current.descent: Descend the southwest face route: roughly 2,000 ft of steep snow and ice up to 65°, downclimbed in good conditions and otherwise rappelled. Below the face, traverse back along the north side of the peak toward Heliotrope Ridge, roped for the glacier, and walk out the Heliotrope Ridge Trail.
current.detailed_rack: Light rack plus many slings for slung blocks/horns; treat all rock and anchors as suspect.
current.pro_needs: Glacier gear for the approach across the Thunder Glacier.

name: X Couloir (Southwest Face) / Standard Route
beta: The historic standard route on Lincoln Peak; the only other line is a rarely formed northwest-face ice route. Approach via Rankin Creek Basin from FS Road 38. Technical snow and ice climbing with significant avalanche risk. Route comprises multiple sections: 30-40 degree initial snowfields, crux serac obstacle requiring 70-85 degree ice climbing (50 feet high), hidden gully with 2-4 foot deep runnels, narrow exposed snow aretes with steep drop-offs, and final 50-degree gully to summit rocks. Climb early morning when snow is frozen; conditions deteriorate rapidly with afternoon warming.
overview: Lincoln Peak's SW Face route, known as the 'X Couloir' (sometimes referenced as 'X Couloir – Emancipation Proclamation'), is the historic line up this seldom-climbed, seriously loose Black Buttes summit. First climbed by Fred Beckey, Wesley Grande, John Rupley, and Herb Staley on July 22, 1956, it was the only documented route to the summit until a 2015 first ascent opened a second line on the NW Face. Only about a dozen ascents are known; the peak is guarded by near-vertical walls on every side.

current.approach: The X Couloir is most directly approached from the south via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38); the less direct alternative starts at Heliotrope Ridge and reaches the southwest face through the Thunder Glacier cirque. Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start hiking/bushwhacking the old decommissioned road around Pt. 4481 toward Rankin Creek — snow travel (often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch) leads past East Rankin Lake (~5,120 ft) and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, near the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. From camp, an alpine start gets the team into the southwest basin and across the bergschrund crux while it's still cold and firm, climbing roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40° snow and a steep serac step in the X Couloir to the 9,085 ft summit. Total approach is on the order of 7 miles and 3,350 ft of gain to the basin camp. Important — access note: FR-38 (Middle Fork Nooksack River Road), damaged in the December 2025 floods, has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since 27 July 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on 25 September 2026, and a separate seasonal gate at Wallace Creek (~mile 10) closes the road December 1-June 15 for elk calving; confirm current road status with the Mount Baker Ranger District (Glacier Public Service Center) before a trip, since the drivable road-end — and therefore the length of the approach — varies year to year.
approach_variant_names: Middle Fork Nooksack Road (FR-38) and Rankin Creek to the treeline camp, then the southwest basin
Heliotrope Ridge and the Thunder Glacier cirque
current.descent: Most parties reverse the ascent line, downclimbing and rappelling the same southwest gully/couloir system (the X Couloir) back down into the southwest basin below the face. This is a real rappelling descent, not a walk-off: the most detailed documented descent (a repeat/'2nd descent' trip report) describes 10 double-rope rappels — 4 off pickets placed by the descending party, 1 off a sling around a rock, and 5 off pre-existing slings left around rock horns lower in the gully. Bring a rope long enough to rappel on doubled strands plus spare cord/webbing for building or backing up anchors, since fixed tat should never be trusted blindly. Anchors are a mix of natural (slung rock horns and blocks) and improvised (snow pickets), not bolted — expect to build some yourself. The exact rappel count is conditions-dependent: earlier-season parties with more continuous snow have gotten down with as few as 3 rappels off deadman/picket anchors and simul-downclimbing between them, while later-season, rockier conditions push the count up toward the 10-rappel figure above; budget for the higher number and extra anchor material. The gully funnels rockfall and is exposed to spindrift/small slides after storms, so descend early and move efficiently through the narrower constrictions. Once off the couloir, re-rope for the bergschrund and any crevassed ground on the way down to the treeline camp, then reverse the approach - down past East Rankin Lake and around Pt. 4481 on the old decommissioned road - back to FR-38. Do not descend north toward Heliotrope Ridge. With a camp in the Rankin Creek basin, going that way puts you on the opposite side of the mountain with a glacier between you and your camp.
current.detailed_rack: Two 60-meter dynamic ropes are standard. Belay anchors use a combination of ice screws (4-6 total; typically #2-#3 Grivel or Black Diamond), natural rock slings, and pickets placed in snow. Most rappel anchors are natural horns slung with webbing or dynamic sling material. Approximately 6-8 pickets for snow anchors.
rack: Small rack: 4 small cams + small nut set
current.pro_needs: Pickets and a light rack; much of the rock is too loose to protect well

name: South Face
beta: The route climbs the gully/face system above a col south of the peak. Parties approach via Ingalls Creek and Crystal Creek to a tarn/col at roughly 7,700-7,880 ft, then scramble ~100 ft of easy Class 3 talus before roping up for two full 60m pitches of low-5th-class granite (a crack/slab pitch, then a rightward traverse into a chimney), finishing with a short Class 3 section through boulders to the summit plateau. One notable hazard is a ~20-ft unprotectable 5.6 slab section below the approach col with no crack systems for gear.
overview: A rarely-climbed, two-pitch 5.5-5.6 rock route straight up Little Annapurna's steep true south face, approached from the seldom-used Ingalls Creek/Crystal Creek side rather than the Enchantments basin.

current.approach: From Highway 97 south of the Y-junction, drive ~7.5 miles and turn onto Ingalls Creek Road/Trailhead. Hike the Ingalls Creek Trail roughly 8 miles, then leave the trail (right/north) into brushy terrain up Crystal Creek, gaining about 2,200 ft to a base-camp meadow and tarn near 6,000 ft. From the tarn, climb a large talus-apron gully west of the tarn to a col at roughly 7,700-7,880 ft between Little Annapurna and the spires to its south.
approach_variant_names: Ingalls Creek and Crystal Creek from the south
current.descent: From the summit plateau, descend north/northeast down talus and slab slopes toward Crystal Lake, then pick up the outlet stream drainage and follow it back down to the Crystal Creek base-camp meadow/tarn, retracing the approach back to Ingalls Creek Trail.
current.detailed_rack: A standard single rack of cams and nuts suffices for the two roped pitches, which offer good crack protection except for one short unprotectable slab move below the approach col.
current.pro_needs: Good protection on both roped pitches (cracks); the crux 20-ft slab section below the col has no protection options and should be approached with caution.

name: North Slopes
beta: From the Stuart/Colchuck Lake Trailhead, hike to Colchuck Lake and grind up the steep boulder-and-scree gully of Aasgard Pass to reach the upper Enchantment basin. From the pass, head roughly south-southwest past Isolation and Tranquil Lakes toward Little Annapurna's northeast ridge, then follow cairns up open granite slabs and talus on the peak's north side to the summit -- one of three rocky high points on the ridge, with the true summit being the middle one. The line itself involves minimal exposure and only occasional Class 3 moves, but Aasgard Pass is the physical and route-finding crux of the day.
overview: Little Annapurna (8,485 ft) is a granite summit in the Core (Upper) Enchantments, Stuart Range, Alpine Lakes Wilderness, immediately south of the Enchantment Lakes basin near Isolation and Tranquil Lakes. It was named by Ellensburg's Sherpa Climbing Club for its resemblance to the Himalayan Annapurna massif. The North Slopes route is the easiest way up the peak, an enjoyable Class 2-3 scramble typically approached via Aasgard Pass, finishing with a short 3rd-class step onto the small summit pedestal and views of Dragontail Peak, the Knitting/Nightmare Needles, and the Enchantment Lakes.

current.approach: From the Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trailhead (~3,500 ft, end of Eightmile Road/FR-7601), follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) about 2.5 miles to the signed fork where the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599.1) splits left/south. Continue roughly 1.8 more miles — crossing Mountaineer Creek and a boulder-hop stretch near the outlet — to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.3 mi in), the last easy, reliable water before the pass. Skirt the lake's south/east shoreline on a braided, cairned climbers' path over talus and slab to the base of Aasgard Pass, the obvious steep gully/headwall at the lake's south end. Aasgard Pass is the crux of the approach: it gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on a mix of dirt switchbacks, loose scree and boulder-hopping, cairns are frequently knocked down and the path braids into several use-trails, and well into summer it can still hold firm snow/ice that makes an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) worthwhile even though the route is otherwise a scramble. Top out at Aasgard Pass (~7,800-7,841 ft, ~5.3 mi from the trailhead). Beyond the pass, cross the grey talus/glacial-till 'moonscape' of the upper Core Zone past Tranquil Lake (Lake Freya) and Isolation Lake, then drop slightly into the meadow-and-tarn complex sometimes called the Brisingamen Lakelets. Near the far end of these meadows watch for an unsigned climbers' path forking right (west) toward Little Annapurna — crossing a stream and passing a toilet sign means you've overshot the junction. From there the route is more a scatter of cairned, well-worn boot paths than a trail; pick the path of least resistance up the broad north-facing slabs and talus on the peak's east/left side, switchbacking and scrambling (low 3rd class at most) to the 8,485-ft summit. Trailhead-to-summit totals run about 15-16 miles and 5,000-5,800 ft. Hazards: no water past the Colchuck Lake outlet, so fill up there; loose rock and rockfall potential on Aasgard Pass and the final slopes, especially with parties above you; full sun/thunderstorm exposure on the open talus above the pass; and early/mid-season snow on the pass creating slip-and-slide fall hazard.
approach_variant_names: Aasgard Pass and the Core, snow-free
Aasgard Pass and the Core with snow
current.descent: Reverse the North Slopes: downclimb the low-3rd-class/class-2 slabs and talus on the peak's east side back to the col/basin, pick up the braided boot paths back through the Brisingamen Lakelets meadows, and rejoin the Core Zone trail past Isolation and Tranquil Lakes to Aasgard Pass. This is a scramble walk-off in both directions — no rope, rack, or rappelling is used on the standard North Slopes line; parties simply describe reversing the ascent, and the peak is often characterized as little more than a steep class 2 hike. The one genuine descent-specific hazard is Aasgard Pass itself: down-climbing its ~2,000 ft of loose scree and talus in the afternoon (often with the sun having softened any remaining snow, and other parties ascending below) is a common cause of rockfall incidents and slips — down-climb deliberately, stay out of others' fall line, and only glissade if a real, clean snow chute with a safe runout is in (by mid-to-late summer the pass is usually bare, exposed talus rather than snow). From the base of the pass, retrace the trail around Colchuck Lake and down the Colchuck Lake/Stuart Lake Trail to the trailhead. Rappels: 0.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is needed.
current.pro_needs: There is no protectable climbing; movement is unroped scrambling. The challenge is minimal beyond basic route-finding and staying back from the south edge.
